utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. It's case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are Monday, the 9th of October, 2006. I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the representatives from the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, and the accused, as well as all the staff members in the courtroom. We shall finish Mr. Kljuic's testimony today, who I would like to greet also. We have planned to hear Mr. Karnavas for 10 minutes so that he can complete his cross-examination. We will then hear Ms. Nozica and Mr. Murphy, who will have an hour and a half between them, and the other Defence counsel will share between them the hour and a half that's left. I would like to state that we must finish at 7.00 today. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours. After careful consideration, having read the record, and seeing that this gentleman is rather difficult to cross-examine under any circumstances, 10 minutes would not be enough for me to accomplish what I wanted to accomplish. Having said that, the points that I wanted to cover can be covered through other witnesses so, therefore, we would not be prejudiced. In light of that, I would yield my time to whoever needs it, and again thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mrs. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to be asking you questions on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Bruno Stojic. When it comes to the councils for certain areas, and I think you know what I'm talking about, the HDZ discussed this for the first time at a Presidency meeting on the 16th of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have Exhibit P 00034, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, these are mostly documents that you've already seen, but we're just going to focus on the councils for the individual areas. It is a Presidency meeting dated the 6th of April, 1991, as we've already said. We have it here. We can assert that that's on page 1. May we have page 3.28 in the Croatian version and page 3 also in the English version. We're going to look at point 2.8, just to remind you, and it says: "According to professional capabilities and affairs which are being conducted, the protagonists for the individual assignments are determined for the individual areas, and it is their duty to rally a team of professional people for the best possible functioning of the party in all fields and to submit a report to the Presidency with a brief programme of work as follows." And here we can see the names. Mr. Mate Boban was in charge of communal affairs; Mr. Ivo -- Iko Stanic was for legal affairs; Vitomir Lukic for culture; Jerko Doko for defence and the police, and so on and so forth. You were in charge of public information together with Ivan Markesic and Smiljko Sagolj. We see that a defence council is formed for defence and the police which will later be called Security Council; am I right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We also see that the criterion was, for the selection of individuals, their professional capabilities and the types of affairs the individual did; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: According to this list, we can see that you adhered to that principle.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that was possible and as far as we were able to find people who were willing to engage.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the organisation of the councils you dealt with at the Presidency meetings, and one of them was on the 10th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have Exhibit P 000341, please. The number was P 0003 -- or, rather, 41. We still don't seem to have the document on our screens. I apologise. It was a Presidency meeting of the Croatian Democratic Community of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 10th of July, 1991. The number is P 00041. It says "341". P 00041. I think we have it now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Those are excerpts from the minutes of the Presidency meeting held on the 10th of July. Now, it is on page 2.2 of the Croatian version, and in English it is page 3. Can we pan down? Yes. Point 2 says: "In order to improve the quality of the work at the level of the HDZ BiH, councils were set up for individual areas. This is necessary in the municipal boards as well and in the municipal board of the HDZ." Then we have the council for the economy. We have a different person here if we compare it to the previous document; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have the security chamber or council. It used to be called the police and security council. Then we have the legal advisory council, the council for culture and education, and the council for health and social welfare. Now, the main point here is, and I think you've already confirmed that, for the first time at this meeting of the Presidency held on the 10th of July, 1991, we have this term "security council" that appears for the first time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, could you just look at what it says above point 2. In the Croatian version, it's on the same page; in English, it is on the following page. 008518890 is the page number. And it says there: "The taking over of power and authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina is a process that still has not been completed for well-known reasons, but work on this must be accelerated at all levels. The takeover of power in BH has not yet been fully completed for well-known reasons," et cetera. Now, was one of the reasons for that, for the fact that you in the HDZ were establishing these councils in the first place, was precisely because power and authority had still not been established after the elections?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons are very complicated why power and authority was not properly established, but it was quite natural that the party which, at that period in time, won 95 per cent of the votes of the Croatian people at the elections had to take into account and take care of some very simple interests - social, health, cultural, economic conditions, and so on and so forth, with a view to the situation in the former Yugoslavia, and of course the security issue. So this was a move on our part by which we wished to compensate for the inertia of the state apparatus, that is to say, to keep us well informed and be in a situation where we could dictate certain solutions in the field, and mostly especially where the Croats were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that this security council was established because of the complex situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina during that period.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, but -- and in Croatia because you had the first incidents that took place at Lake Plitvice and then the sabotage in Borovo Selo where Croatian policemen were killed. But there was general tension, very high tension. There was a lot of propaganda. Milosevic had control of the television and the media. He had the army and the police. So that we had to react and prepare for that situation. And if you were better organised, then you were better prepared and better able to deal with the situation. Of course, all this depended on the geographical and political position of the individual regions as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, the HDZ board, at its meeting of the 6th of August, did it also deal with these councils and, in fact, supported the conclusion made by the Presidency to appoint the councils of the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I have Exhibit P 00047 now, please. Yes, we have it here in front of us. Let's just see whether it is the minutes. May we look at page 5.14 in the Croatian version, and it is page ERN number 00337302 in the English version. Also point 14. I'm sure you'll be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, as we're looking at the Croatian version first of all, I'd like to draw your attention to point 14. It says: "The Main Board of the BH HDZ confirms the resolutions of the BH HDZ Presidency of the 10th of July, 1991, about the appointment of councils and persons in charge, respectively." And we have the same composition of the councils. And then: "It is important to mention that the persons in charge must immediately," as it says, "submit the lists of persons whom they propose for council members to the secretariat of the BH HDZ." We can conclude on that basis, Mr. Kljuic, can we not, that the members of the council still had not been appointed; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, as to the councils for individual areas or departments, that was dealt with on the 26th of August at the Presidency meetings; 1991, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have the next exhibit, P 00052 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We can see the first page, and on that first page it says the following - and this is something that is frequently mentioned at the meetings that you presided over - that Mr. Ante Beljo was present. Can you tell us who Mr. Ante Beljo as at the point in time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Beljo was the general secretary of the Croatian Democratic Community of the Croatian Republic, who came to Bosnia often to hold consultations and sometimes following directives. And he was rather close to us because he was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So in Zagreb they probably put him in charge of being this liaison between our two parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we take a look at something we're interested in now which relates to the councils, which is to be found on page 2.4 in the Croatian and page 2 of the English version as well. The ERN number is 00860077. So it's the following page of the English version, point 4. Next page. And it says: "On behalf of the HDZ BH Presidency, the following are appointed to the councils." And now for the first time we see who made up the councils. We're interested in the security council now. That's what I'd like to focus on. There's your name; there's Mate Boban, Branko Kvesic. What was Branko Kvesic at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Kvesic was the Assistant Minister for the Interior and the head of the department which was once known as UDBA, U-D-B-A, or rather the security service, which was a very important segment in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Jerko Doko was the Defence Minister; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And the rest of the people there all had some sort of relationship with defence and dealt with defence and security, which is what the security council did.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the representatives of regions. Filipovic was from Samac; this other man, Bozo Rajic, was from another place, and so on. So we included people who held these regional positions and covered all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You had a representative of Herzegovina, Posavina, and people working in the state administration, such as Jerko Doko and myself, because I was also a member of the state council for security, ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now we come to the conclusions from the HDZ BH Security Council meeting held on the 18th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have the next document. It is P 00058. The first page of that document, both in English and in B/C/S. Yes, there is it is. We have page 1. Can we just pan down, yes, so that we can see the whole of the first page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Here we see that the Security Council co-opted Bruno Stojic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And as you testified, he was the Assistant Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Assistant to the Minister of the Interior Affairs, and he was in charge of the financial department and logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. For material resources.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So he was elected after the multi-party elections to occupy that post. He was elected by the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't in the electoral process, but he was appointed on behalf of the HDZ which, among other things, in dividing up power -- in the power division, was given that function. And then recommendations came in, we held consultations, and he was appointed assistant minister for the interior with the departments that you mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was that position the reason that he was appointed to this body?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At this session, the security council changed its name to the Crisis Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you remember whether any other sessions of this Crisis Staff were held, attended by Bruno Stojic and that you attended, too?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say whether a session was held but the Crisis Staff functioned in Sarajevo because all the deputies in power were members of the Crisis Staff. Jerko Doko, myself and many others, Brana Kvesic, we communicated with each other on a daily basis. You must be familiar with the time period that we are referring to now. There was a war in Croatia or an aggression had been launched against Croatia, a full-scale war. In Bosnia, non-Serbs were being expelled from the territory. There were many refugees that had to be taken care of, assisted. The Crisis Staff received relevant information and then we tried to intervene with the JNA. For example, we'd receive news that Croats had been expelled from a village in the vicinity of Prijedor. We then had to check that information. We visited our police force. Sometimes we went to see the federal police as well. We then contacted Kadijevic, the Minister of Defence. The Crisis Staff had the task of trying to assist those who were at risk at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So I can draw the conclusion that there was unofficial contact that took place frequently. Because of the dynamics of the events, you tried to solve the problems. You'd communicate with the members that you managed to contact; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And sometimes the members, without the president himself, tried to resolve certain problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the course of your examination-in-chief, you already testified, as stated in this document, that it was the duty of the Crisis Staff to remain in charge of the entire system of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I ask you again many times before that please kindly slow down, both of you, Ms. Nozica and also Mr. Kljuic. If I may ask you to speak a bit more slowly and to stop when one of you asks a question or answering a question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I do apologise, Your Honour. I'll try to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the course of the examination-in-chief, you said that it was the duty of the Crisis Staff to control the entire defence system for the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was their duty to obtain weapons, and this is what this document, in fact, states under item 1, paragraph 3, of the conclusion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was our desire. As to whether we were successful, I couldn't say because the task was too immense for people who were, in fact, amateurs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As far as you know, at that point in time had the Muslims started being armed through the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, and had they started to organise them? Just a minute. Could you wait for the interpretation, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? I'm not sure that it was organised in the way that they say today and that people are now asking for pensions on that basis. But that people were spontaneously armed well, there is no doubt about that. Everyone was arming themselves. And I must say that the main sources for weapons were local; that is to say, there were Serbian paramilitary formations and individuals from the JNA who were involved in trafficking weapons and selling weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we continue to discuss what you know about the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. Were these units organised, and was the public aware of that? Did you know about that in 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in the way that they say now, but there were groups that were interlinked, that were organised, that were preparing themselves for the defence of the homeland. That was visible and you could see that in Sarajevo when the aggression was launched. Had such youths not existed, Sarajevo would probably have fallen. It wouldn't have been able to resist for 320 days to the siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When we're talking about the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, then we're talking about a Muslim organisation, about SDA military units.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to say that among those groups that defended Sarajevo, well, there were people of various ethnic groups. First of all, I should have to tell you something about certain social categories that were represented. They were all poor people, and there were some pre-war delinquents who participated in the defence of the homeland, while Marxist intellectuals and others just waited to see what would happen. These young people had some very positive qualities. Later there were certain problems, certain deviations, but that was the problem of the system, it wasn't a problem with the youth. These young people from Sarajevo often defended the town. In spite of the fact that they were so poorly equipped, I think they should be given credit for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We do agree that at that very beginning there were people who had been organised by the police. There were people who, as you say, had organised themselves, but in addition there were also people who had already become members of the Patriotic League Bosna and the Green Berets. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you perhaps familiar with a meeting of Muslim representatives from Bosnia and Herzegovina or, rather, from the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia, a meeting that was held in the home of the police in Sarajevo on the 10th of June, 1991? And at this meeting a council for national defence was established which functioned under the SDA.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, but the Serbs had a Crisis Staff under the SDS and we had formed a Crisis Staff, so naturally the Muslims would do the same. That was to be expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you are now telling me that at this time each people, under the parties that represented them, tried to organise themselves and prepare themselves for the war that was imminent.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that you remember that at the time the JNA changed its image. It was no longer the people's army, it was the Serbs' army. And it went a step further. Under Veljko Kadijevic, it was no longer a communist and socialist force; it ended up being a Chetnik army. At the time, terrible war crimes were being committed in Croatia, as well as in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it was quite natural that the Ministry of Defence of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, was in control of the situation. So the people organised themselves as they could and everything was secret. So it was done on a national and religious basis, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At the Presidency sessions, did you discuss these matters with other members? Did you discuss the arming of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, citizens of all three ethnic groups? Because there was the threat of Serbia and Montenegro launching an aggression.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that at that time Bosnia and Herzegovina felt very tense. There was a lot of tension, because the communist government, immediately prior to the first democratic elections, handed over the weapons of the Territorial Defence to the JNA. That was because of the judges. Josip Broz established a system of military formations that included the JNA, which was the regular military force composed of professional soldiers, but there was another system, that of the Territorial Defence. It was a sort of William Tell force. The people were armed and this force existed in order to conduct a guerrilla war.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Kljuic. I think the Trial Chamber has already heard much about the system of Territorial Defence from other witnesses. I think they know what the Territorial Defence was. But when the JNA took over these weapons from the Territorial Defence, didn't Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, who was the President of the Presidency, object to this at the time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right. The weapons were handed over before the first democratic elections were held. The socialist government, the Presidency, allowed this, not the new democratically elected government. We arrived once the weapons had already been handed over, once they had already taken these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you arrived, as you put it, were there any official reactions on the part of Mr. Izetbegovic? Because those weapons were, in a certain sense, still in Bosnia-Herzegovina; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the weapons were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they were under the control of the JNA and the Serbian forces. Later, generals, such as General Zelac in Banja Luka, distributed these to the citizens in Krajina. Izetbegovic did not publicly object because he believed that the JNA would not attack Bosnia and Herzegovina, would not launch an aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina. But there were people who mentioned this issue. But you must also be aware of the fact that the media was under the control of the communists. That was not just the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian communists had also handed over the weapons to the JNA, and the only communists in the former Yugoslavia who hadn't handed over their weapons were the Slovenians, because they were primarily Slovenians and then there were Yugoslavs and members of the international community. But in our country, to be a Yugoslav was more important than to be a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at least that was the opinion of those in top positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I want to go back to a certain subject and link it to your answer, according to which Mr. Izetbegovic didn't publicly protest. You can't say that when the newly elected democratic government was appointed they were not in a position to react in public.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Minister of Defence, Jerko Doko, did react, but it was all to no avail. That's quite irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is that irrelevant or is that the SDA's -- the SDA party's attitude to the war that was imminent? That wasn't the case for the HDZ, because you're talking about Jerko Doko. Is that something that would be important when it comes to this difference in reactions?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The Croats -- national consciousness among the Croats was more developed. They could hardly wait to leave Yugoslavia. Whereas in the case of the Muslims, whom we call Bosniaks now, this consciousness was not that developed. On the other hand, there were many Muslim citizens, not only from Bosnia and Herzegovina but also from Sandzak and from Montenegro, who were members of the JNA or the police force, the secret services and all other bodies that were loyal to the regime. They would need a lot of time. It was only once they started killing them it would take them a lot of time to realise that the JNA was not a people's army. And then the resistance movement among the Muslims began developing, began to strengthen. And they were the greatest victims in the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you said that the Territorial Defence handed over its weapons to the JNA before the democratic elections, do you remember a few months prior to that event what the situation was like?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had our elections in October and November; Croatia in May. So this was even before the elections in Croatia. I am referring to the year 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. My information was somewhat different. We were discussing the Patriotic League. I'd like to know now, today, you have any information, according to which such units had been formed in Banja Luka, in Trebinje. And were the people who were members of the Patriotic League in Mostar, Konjic, Zenica? This is the territory where the Serbian party was predominant; am I right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. No one formed military formations in a territory where they were in the minority. The Serbs didn't do that in Travnik either, although there were 19 per cent Serbs there. Everyone obtained weapons illegally, and Belgrade did this in docile. I'll explain it later. They formed such units where they were in the majority and where they had a certain amount of security, where they could act in secrecy. Belgrade had to have an alibi in order to launch an aggression. So they spread propaganda and claimed that the Croats and Muslims had armed themselves. And if you have a look at the print from the year 1990 or 1991, if you have a look at Ekspres Politika, Nin, they write that the Serbs were under threat because the Ustasha have armed themselves; how the counter-intelligence service in Yugoslavia deliberately sold ordinary weapons, pistols and rifles, so that the Croats and the Muslims could give the impression that they had armed themselves. And this was a handicap because some people really believed that they had armed themselves. Then in Croatia the situation was different. They could import weapons from the West. That wasn't the case in Bosnia. So there wasn't a sufficient amount of weapons, and the state couldn't defend the citizens because, according to the law, we could only strengthen the police force. I must say, the professional police force was the most capable force. Later there were divisions in the police force and the Serbs went their own way. But the legally appointed authorities, the legally appointed government, we tried to mobilise about 30 or 40.000 reserve policemen, and they received weapons because the police had weapons in their warehouse. And the then Minister of the Interior, on the 31st of March, 1992, disbanded the reserve police force ostensibly because there wasn't enough money to finance it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there's been a mistake on page 16, line 17. It said "90 per cent" Serbs when the witness was referring to the number of Serbs in Travnik, but the witness said "19 per cent". So that is a big difference and we have to put that right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, thank you for mentioning the police, because you were thinking of the structure in which Mr. Bruno Stojic worked, is that right, during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bruno Stojic was an economist. He had no political and I don't think he had any military influence in the military. He was the quartermaster. He procured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It was MTS.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he procured weapons, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you're saying was distributed in a professional way and in a fairly proper way. That's what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police was multi-ethnic. It was proportionate, the ratio was proportionate to the population make-up. And that was important because, with dozens of thousands of weapons that all the citizens had, the aggression would have been a little -- would have been even worse, especially since the professional policemen were reduced in number. We had a situation where people who had come to defend Bosnia took up arms and knew nothing about weapons, especially when the new complicated weapons came into play. And so there were a lot of casualties. People were not well-trained and well-versed in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I am looking at the transcript, so I'm following what you're saying and looking at the transcript. Well, I don't see why you're avoiding an answer to the question. Was it the same police, or, rather, the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in which Mr. Bruno Stojic worked at the time? Is it the same ministry? You're talking about the police force that was a professional police force.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was one of the assistant ministers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to hear. Now, I'm not going to show you the last document from this series of documents relating to the security council, but I am going to remind you that at a meeting of the 16th of January, 1992, the security situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was discussed again. It was on the agenda. And it was stated again that the Crisis Staffs of the BH at all levels must work immediately and urgently in the sphere of defence preparation. Now, you've said that this was a complex process and that you couldn't expect to have satisfactory results during such a short period of time. Then it was logical that this was an ongoing task that had to be done and that the Presidency referred to and took care of. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to another area. I'd just like to remind you that during your testimony earlier on, in response to a question from Judge Antonetti on the 27th of June, 2006, when you were asked why you did not convene an HDZ party convention at the end of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992, you were asked to explain your position. And this is on pages 3922 and 3 of the transcript. You said, your answer was, that you couldn't convene a convention because of the siege of Sarajevo at the time, because communication from Sarajevo was made very much more difficult. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there was no need for me to call a regular convention.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'd like to ask you to focus on what I'm asking you and to focus on the siege of Sarajevo at the blockade.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But let me just say that there was no need, because, on the 23rd and 24th of March, 1991, I did have a convention in Mostar but because of different political situations and obstruction within the HDZ, it said, of my right wing, on the part of the right wing people, it was necessary to say what our aim was. But I wasn't able to do that because of the situation that Sarajevo was facing and also because those overruled at the convention in Mostar didn't want to go forward because they knew they wouldn't win.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you've explained that to us in detail. I'd just like to remind you of the portion of your testimony where you referred to the blockade, the siege of Sarajevo, which was still in force -- which was in force at the time and which meant that Sarajevo could not communicate with the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, during that period of time, or, let's say, from April 1992 onwards, did the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Presidency itself, did they have any control? Were they able to communicate with the rest of the territory which was not occupied at that time by the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as communication is concerned, that was possible with individual areas. It was made more difficult, of course, but -- and of course, there were isolated territories where you couldn't communicate and others which refused to follow the orders of the central government or adhere to the central government.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, faced in a situation like that with Sarajevo under siege, was it possible for the government or Presidency - and did they, in fact, do anything - to assist in the defence of Mostar, to defend it from the Serb army in May, 1990? Were they technically able to do so? And do you know whether they did anything?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from moral support, we could do nothing at that time. Not only support to Mostar but to Tuzla or Gorazde or Bihac either. And faced with a situation like that, people had to look to themselves and organise themselves. And, of course, with that self-organisation, the question was were they loyal to the regular powers or not? The Serb areas refused to pledge allegiance to the central government. They were not loyal to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we'll deal with that later on. During my cross-examination, we'll deal with the question of loyalty to the legal powers that be and the legal government. But for the moment I'd like to dwell on what you analysed and said a moment ago and told the Trial Chamber, in fact, in explaining the situation with the Presidency and government at that time. Now, do you happen to remember that there were some government meetings that were held in Zagreb, Bosnia-Herzegovinian government meetings were held in Zagreb, because it was technically easier than it was to hold them in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say for the benefit of the Trial Chamber that Bosnia-Herzegovina experienced two ills; one was the aggression and the other was treachery within the people in power. Because you have to know that people fled from the Presidency and government.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you mean from all three ethnic groups, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Five Muslim ministers with the vice premier left the government, stepped down from the government. The Serbs did, too, although not all of them. The Vice Premier Simovic stayed on for a certain time, but the Minister of Justice stayed on in Sarajevo throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If I seem to be a little nervous, it's because my -- I have time constraints, so that's why I'm trying to move on. Do you know, for example, that some SDA meetings were held during that period of time in Zagreb, for instance?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. But that they had strong headquarters or staff in Zagreb, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That the SDA had a strong headquarters in Zagreb; what do you mean by that? Or staff.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had people dealing with logistics, with the economy, and so on, and they were in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we say that that was throughout the period during the war? And what about the logistics base in Split?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps most of it was in Vienna, for example, and so on and so forth. Of course there was a theory according to which you couldn't -- people thought that you couldn't help Bosnia-Herzegovina from Sarajevo, that you had to go outside. But then the people who said that, who were putting out that kind of slogan, were people who had already left BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. In Vienna we had the main logistics base when it came to a question of money, but I'm interested in Croatia, myself. I would like to look at Croatia. So you can focus on that. So can you tell me whether you know that both in Split and Zagreb there were strong logistics bases of the BH army, precisely the BH army?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, during 1992 and the beginning of 1993, for instance, on behalf of the government - and I'm talking about 1992 and the beginning of 1993, as I said - that on behalf of the government and the Presidency of the BH, key decisions were taken by the representatives of the Bosniak people. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot agree with that. But that they were the most numerous, that is right, that is correct. Now, I don't know what decisions you have in mind. Decisions of principle, which were taken by the Presidency, was taken by consensus of the people who remained in Sarajevo. Now, as far as the government is concerned, those prime ministers would go. They left Sarajevo. They would very often act against the government. There was a prime minister that had fled and worked against Bosnia-Herzegovina, its interests.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the main decisions, the key decisions, in fact, that the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina depended, the positions taken with respect to the peace agreements, for example, and the decisions of interest to all three ethnic groups, in fact. Because you, several times yourself, said that Mr. Izetbegovic -- and Mr. Izetbegovic during his lifetime said many times that you strove for a multi-national, multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, those decisions, which were key decisions for those citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina of multi-ethnicity and linked to the agreements and contacts with the international community, so on and so forth, positions taken when people went to attend those conferences, were they taken at the level of the entire Presidency or were they taken within the frameworks of a very small number of people who were politically linked to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that the referendum for independence, in order to gain independence and become a member of the United Nations, were decisions which we took jointly. I took part in the process myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I am referring to the period after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I said specifically from April onwards up until the time you were active in the Presidency. And when was that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 10th of October, 1992, and then from the 4th of November, 1993, again until the 15th of October, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, let's take that entire period. What would your appraisal be?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say, first of all, that I was not a member of those delegations and that's for two reasons; one was that Mr. Izetbegovic did not like me; and secondly, that Tudjman didn't want to receive the Bosnian delegation if I was there, regardless of the fact that I was the legitimate representative of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Why didn't Izetbegovic like you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they all said that they were in favour of a multi-ethnic bourgeois Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said that I was in favour of a multi-national one with citizens rights in order to represent citizens interests. And I have remained along that course to the present day. Now, why Bosnia's no longer a multi-national community, a multi-ethnic community which we fought for, as the communists like to say, there are subjective factors and objective factors to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. I'm not trying to appear naive in any way, but if Mr. Izetbegovic fought for a multi-ethnic --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I never said that. He did declare himself in favour of that. However, he allowed Haris Silajdzic to introduce a delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina into the United Nations with four Muslims. And I said, "Gentlemen, I would have found at least one Serb," even if he was a main Serb and this blind Croat and made him a member of that. So because of my views in the Presidency I encountered a great deal of problems, and they sold me out. When they went to the London conference, they took a clerk with them; he would later on become a political personage but was never elected anywhere. But they didn't take me on behalf of the Croats. Why? Because all those staff members and clerks would nod their heads throughout the whole aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina. Ivo, my neighbour, didn't take me with the delegation because I was a true fighter for a multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, the fact that I did not succeed is no fault of my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Very well. But I wanted to show you an opinion that Lord Owen had at the time, or, rather, Lord Owen's opinion at that time, and you seem to confirm that, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may we look at 2D 00191. That's the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me just tell you it's an excerpt from the Balkan Odyssey by Lord Owen, the presiding person over the international conference on Yugoslavia. I'm sure you met him a number of times yourself and I'm sure you read the book.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is yes to both questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we look at page 85 in the Croatian version now, please, and page 52 of the English version. 52, please, Balkan Odyssey. I have underlined the portion of the text that I'm going to read out, and I gave the interpreters a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have a copy at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit number is 2D 00191.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So the --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to read out the portion that is underlined: "When the Croat Mile Akmadzic was appointed Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have received a copy of the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to read it slowly. "When the Croat Mile Akmadzic was appointed Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he made a real effort to revive the collective leadership of the Presidency. He went back to live in Sarajevo and used his previous experience as pre-war secretary to the Presidency to try to restore the authority of the Muslim-Croat coalition that had won the referendum on independence which the Serbs boycotted. "But by the end of 1992, it was becoming clear to all that he would fail and that power had gone to a small group of Muslim ministers appointed by President Izetbegovic and their nominee as vice-president, Ejup Ganic. The collective presidency, as a democratic body with meaningful representation from the constituent nations, was, by the autumn of 1993, no longer a reality. The real decisions were made elsewhere. We were, in effect, dealing with a Muslim government for a predominantly Muslim population." Can we have your comments to this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Lord Owen is not a proper witness. He was not objective. And secondly, the result that Izetbegovic had taken over power was not only his desire but he received great support from Zagreb. What I mean to say is this: I was supposed to be the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 19th of December, 1992, pursuant to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then there was a secret agreement by which I was eliminated from the Presidency. And in the name of the Croats, a man was brought in who had never taken part at the elections, and that was because of this secret agreement between Izetbegovic and Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Were you familiar with that secret agreement?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A friend of mine from Zagreb, a member of the Croatian leadership, Slavko Degoricija, informed me through a woman in Rijeka that something was being prepared against me, but the woman couldn't tell me what. But the agreement found itself to be justified, was justified, in a sense, because Izetbegovic, in attempt to be the president of the Presidency, on the 19th of December, 1992, rejected the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Please let me finish. President Tudjman was aware of the fact. So in January 1993 - and at the time I was just an ordinary citizen of Sarajevo - at a meeting in Zagreb he told me, he said, "Mr. Izetbegovic, you're familiar with the constitution of your country. You're not the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You're the president of the Muslims and as such you are welcome." So for all those who tried to topple Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Milosevic and others, what was important is that the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been rejected.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I don't want to go into the reasons for these issues at the moment, but it is true, you can't deny this, that whatever Mr. Tudjman wanted, Mr. Izetbegovic eliminated you from the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally. It wasn't Tudjman. Tudjman asked Izetbegovic to do something that he couldn't do himself. He acted pro domo sua. He wanted to -- but, in fact, he betrayed the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was only in autumn, 1993, as mentioned in Owen's book, it was only then, when the legally elected leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been completely eliminated, it was only then, at the insistence of the international community, that he would come to see me and we would again establish a multi-national body. However, the Presidency no longer had power. Individuals had power. There were negotiations with the Muslim side at all times. And if a Croat or a Serb appeared as the seventh dwarf in those delegations, none would ask him about anything. As soon as no one asked me for my opinion I didn't participate in such matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Nonetheless, you were a member of the Presidency until 1996, and now that you've mentioned this, I would like to know, since you said Muslims sometimes participated in negotiations, does this confirm that Mr. Izetbegovic, or someone who sent him to the negotiations, after 1993, after your return, did he always represent the Bosniaks and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. They took this into account so they had Lazovic and Komsic as the representatives of the Serbs and the Croats. But whenever there was a summit or negotiations, for example, Washington or Dayton, the Presidency would establish a framework for the political issues that should be addressed, issues that should represent the minimum interests of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As to whether they protected these interests and interpreted them as such, I don't know. I didn't participate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like you, Mr. Kljuic, to clarify something in your previous answer. You refer to "he" and you say "he betrayed," that is on line 3, page 28. "He betrayed the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and later on you say, "He would come to see me and we would again establish a multi-national body." That would be line 7 and 8. Who is "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "He" is President Izetbegovic, but what follows is not something that I said. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to the subject of the ABiH. We're talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Before we move on to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'd like to clarify something you said a minute ago; that there was an agreement between Tudjman and Izetbegovic in order for you to be eliminated from the Presidency, because, according to what you said, you should have been the president of the Presidency. Why did Tudjman eliminate you as being president of the Presidency, a Croat, when you could have been an advantage for him? What was, in fact, at stake when you were eliminated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, according to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, seven members of the Presidency are full equal, and the president of the Presidency is primus inter pares, the first among equals. According to the constitution, one individual can be the president of the Presidency for two years at most. There are elections every year, so there can be -- he can have two terms of office. Mr. Izetbegovic was elected in 1990, and his mandate ended on the 19th of December, 1992. That was the ultimate deadline. At the time of communism, the order of rotation for the president of the Presidency had been established. First there would be a Serb, then a Muslim or Bosniak, and then a Croat. So I was next in line to be the president of the Presidency. Your Honour, you have claimed that President Tudjman would have found it advantageous to have me in such a position. That's my position, too. However, he decided not to take advantage of having me in such an advantageous position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your opinion, why did he take such a decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was a favourite of us for a certain period of time. But as I am an individual who was not susceptible to suggestions, I always followed my own line. And I also noticed that in Zagreb and in Belgrade they had no love for Bosnia and Herzegovina, nor did they understand Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then thirdly, as a legally elected Croatian member of the Presidency, I obtained half a million votes and not a single Croat had obtained that many votes before me or after I had left. But in that capacity, I believe that the defence of a multi-national and secular Bosnia-Herzegovina was my historical task. When certain policy changes had been carried out in Zagreb, I was removed. I would say that perhaps Mr. Tudjman wanted me to be politically removed but he didn't want me to be killed. There were others who threatened to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we have to go back to that situation. Did Mr. Izetbegovic remove you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You assume that this was done following suggestions made by Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Izetbegovic removed me from the Presidency. That's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you left the Presidency, when the term of office expired --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My term of office did not expire.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please let me finish. When Mr. Izetbegovic's first term of office expired, was there anyone else, who was not a Bosniak, who could have been the president of the Presidency? Did he remove you because Tudjman had requested that, or was it so that he could hold on to power? He did hold on to power, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The Presidency was changing in legal terms. That happened when the Serbian representatives left the Presidency, Mrs. Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That was in April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others were appointed on the basis of votes; that was quite legitimate. But I was removed, they brought in someone else who didn't participate in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If a Croatian member of the Presidency should have become president of Presidency and you had been removed for political reasons, then why didn't this person become the president? Why did Mr. Izetbegovic hold on to power until the very end?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Izetbegovic didn't remove me in order to appoint a new individual. He removed me in order to hold on to power.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. I think we have clarified this issue now. Before the break, let us just move on to another series of interesting questions that relate to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In your opinion, did the Presidency at that time have control over the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we assumed power, it was just before the celebration of the day of the army of Yugoslavia, and since each republic had its own celebrations, the leadership of the army in Bosnia and Herzegovina had already been marginalised at the time. As weapons were being taken from the Territorial Defence, at the same time Veljko Kadijevic reorganised army areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kljuic, I really have very limited time. I don't want to be impolite. I'm referring to the period April, 1992, just before the events of April. I'm referring to your participation in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no control over the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm referring to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was formed from the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So perhaps there was a misunderstanding. I'm asking you whether you had any control over the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did the Presidency have such control? Did they listen to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Absolutely. Very well. Have you heard about a meeting in Zenica in August, 1993? I know you weren't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there and I've heard nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Later, when you became a member of the Presidency towards the end of 1993 again, did you have the opportunity of hearing about the attitudes of the army brass with regard to the Presidency and the government?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when I returned - how to point this out - the Presidency no longer had control over the finance sector and the army. We had very little information. There was no weapons. There was no food.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I had returned in 1993, in autumn.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From 1993 onwards?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Control of the army had been taken over, and over the police. The Presidency was powerless. And I should also point out that the members of the Presidency weren't really interested in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Power had been taken over -- power had been taken over over the army and the police. From whom? By whom?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 2D 00187, conclusions from the meeting in Zenica. I believe that you will find this interesting. Have a look at some of these conclusions that also concern the period during which you were in the Presidency. We'll have a look at the first page for a moment. Have a look at the first page. Item 2, these are conclusions: "The goals of our army's struggle remain: The struggle for a State of Bosnia-Herzegovina which shall remain unified and within its recognised borders." We're talking about the 21st and 22nd of August, 1993. Have a look at item 3: "The war for territory will continue. Even if there is peace along the lines of the Geneva Agreement, the continuation of the war will be against both ..." And then could we have a look at the following page in English and in Croatian: "... will be against both forms of Fascism, the Serbian-Montenegrin one and the Ustasha one, whether taken separately or together." Let's have a look at another conclusion on page 3, page 3 in the English version and in the Croatian version. Item 11, it says: "The civilian and military authorities during this period of time, when fighting was ongoing, were not acting in accordance with the main principles of armed combat. The civilian powers only partly engaged in war, which resulted in not acting in a functional, moral, and logistical way." It's not important how this continues. Let's have a look at 3: "In all corps, use offensive operations in skirmishes and combats more than previously. Sabotage and reconnaissance operations are to acquire a mass character focusing on the enemy's shallow and deep rear."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness the last page in English and in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The document was signed by the deputy commander of the Main Staff of the armed forces, Sefer Halilovic. The top brass who participated at this meeting first accused the civilian authorities for not having helped them arm themselves. Given the document we have just seen, is this a conclusion that can be drawn?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think so. They were unhappy because they hadn't been provided with the finance that they needed by local communes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We'll come to that later on. But may we just take a look at something that's very important for you and your activities in the Presidency, the discussion by Mr. Sefer Halilovic at the meeting in Zenica on the 21st and 22nd of August, 1993. And that is Exhibit 2D 00186. It is the transcript of this meeting, the consultations held. It is page 21 in the Croatian version and 20 in the English. And I have underlined for Their Honours and the interpreters the portion I wish to read out. I think they have that. I'll be reading slowly. It is on page 21. I think they have -- we have the page. And I'd like to focus on the middle of the page downwards. I'm going to start and read: "I have to say here I'm sorry that there are no members of the Presidency here so that I don't end up talking about them behind their backs. The state has neither purchased for us nor obtained for us even the minimum of weapons and ammunition, not even when the routes were open, completely open. In the first five months, Sule ..." I assume you know who "Sule" is, the Sule referred to. It was Mr. Sulejman Vranje, we can see from the transcript. "... you could get through without any major fuss, without any problems, and then in the following five months you could get through with some certification. Some would say yes, some no, but some got through. Well, then it was blocked and there was no way at all. There's no way at all now. Thus the state did not obtain anything for us, even when it was possible, because they were privatising public property and public resources. It was privatisation, pure and simple. "After 13 victims in Sarajevo, from my close family members, I no longer have any intention of not telling anyone in this state what I think of them, even if it costs me my life that very second, costs me my life that instance. I have no private interest in anyone, but I have an interest in the survival of the state and the people. We have the privatisation of resources. Some very exclusive groups of people are occupied with that and we don't get any benefit from that. We're left with the question of how and by what methods we can acquire booty, how and in what way we can get large installations into operation for the special purpose industry. How to take Vitez and how to take Zunovnica, because for our army, they are two strategic features, with Vitez, the military industry system of our state comes full circle. Then it is complete. Then we have the complete chain in our hands." I'm going to stop there for a moment. Mr. Kljuic, who were you taking -- who was Vitez being taken from? Where was it? Serbia? Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Bosnia-Herzegovina where Croatian power and authority was exercised during the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We can continue now. Thank you. "In Zunovnica we get to what is super urgent, to what is ready, to what could be used immediately. The raw materials, the TNT is there. There is gunpowder. There are weapons and ammunition. And with Vitez, we integrate the entire special purpose production system. If the question would be: Now your house is on fire. Do you put out the house fire or take Vitez? I would go for Vitez first. With Vitez we integrate the entire special purpose production." Now, the weapons via the Green Berets and Patriotic League and so on, can you tell us when that was? 1993? On the last page is Sefer Halilovic's contribution. It is page 22 of the Croatian and 21 in the English. I'd just like to read out one important sentence. So page 22 for the Croatian and 21 for the English. I'll read it out. It's in the lower section, towards the end. It says: "I must tell you that Bakir Alispahic and Sule and this group of people, I'm certain, armed the Sarajevo region, the Eastern Bosnia region in the pre-war period, as a member of the Patriotic League. We moved about that, fled, hid, made arrests." So we see there -- and Vitez is going to be very important, because after the break I'm going to ask you about what you said at the Presidency meeting in referring to Vitez and your opposition to taking control of Vitez. But from what we've just read out, can we see from that that, in actual fact, the main person in command was criticising the authorities for the lack of weapons, and, on the other hand, stating an intention to continue, regardless -- to continue the war regardless of whether a peace treaty would be signed or not. And was that the general mood that prevailed at the time, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am going to object. This, once again, hasn't been a question but a speech. Is the question to the witness, has she read it correctly out loud to him, or does he have any knowledge other than what's been read to him in this document? The witness has already said he was not involved in the government during this time period, from October of 1992 until November of 1993. He specifically was not in this meeting. So we spent the last 10 or 15 minutes doing a long reading by counsel. Does this witness have any personal knowledge, beyond pure speculation, as to what this meeting means or what was said or what the policy of these people were? There is no foundation whatsoever, except if he wants to say -- if she wants to say, "Did I read this correctly?" Then I suppose all of us in the courtroom who have followed along can say, "Yes, you read it correctly." Other than that, there's no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Nozica, the witness, in the month of August, was not part of the Presidency again. This meeting was held on the 21st and 22nd of August. You quoted a part of the text in which Sefer Halilovic seemed to be criticising the political figures who had not made available to the ABiH army all the resources that were necessary. He talks about privatisation, and seems to imply that some political personalities may have had a personal interest in this and may not have only considered the interest of the state. The witness was not a member of the Presidency at that time, so what do you want to ask him about? You want to ask him about a meeting which he did not attend? He certainly had no knowledge at the time of Halilovic's discourse. So what is the point you want to make here?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Halilovic at this meeting presented his views about the work of the Presidency before the beginning of the conflict and right up to that particular month of August. Now, since the witness, until the end of 1992, was in the Presidency, then the question was whether it was clear to him that the army, BH army, held such positions. Because the army here is assessing a longer period, not just the last eight months but a longer period of time. So I'm asking him whether he was aware of that while he was in the Presidency and whether he knew about it when he returned to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not aware of that. I did not know about it, because the army had become transformed since its inception up until the period that Halilovic is referring to. And I have to say that I contributed to having Halilovic become commander, because at that time we had top-ranking officers who were Serbs and Croats; they were loyal to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm talking about Jovo Divjak and Stjepan Siber. And we had a third officer, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, an Italian, who was a very capable officer but who did not suit the functionaries of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was an individual who did not carry his religious feelings on his sleeve. On the other hand, Halilovic, at the beginning, was Izetbegovic's favourite. Later on, he was openly hostile to him. But Halilovic was a low-ranking officer, and in 1991 he was still a captain. He obtained the rank of major just a few months later. So he threw him out and carried on with his communist rhetorics, and said that Zagreb and Belgrade were the same vis-a-vis Bosnia-Herzegovina, which wasn't true at all. Croatia received half a million Muslims. It took in others, too. It helped them, sent them further on into the world. On the other hand, Mr. Izetbegovic took his family to Brac, the island of Brac, and did not take them to Gornji Milanovac, for example. And that's the best answer to those people who still say today that Zagreb and Belgrade were equated, that they were equally hostile to Bosnia-Herzegovina. We fought against that, but there you have it. You see the captain of a Yugoslav People's Army speaking in that way. On the other hand, perhaps this was something that was not known to the public, but the Croats were the bad guys in the Muslim place and the Muslims were the good guys. But it was standard practice for people walking around. Today, when we looked at some papers, we find that Mr. Tudjman wasn't the sole individual to blame for the conflict with the Muslims and Izetbegovic. Just as Izetbegovic said once that you need two to go to war; then you need two for everything. And in writing my book quite recently, "The Betrayal of Bosnia," I came upon an agreement between Mr. Izetbegovic and Boban, which was signed in front of Lord Owen, saying that the Bosnian republic would have an exit to the Adriatic Sea, and apart from that, that it would have a guaranteed status of a naval -- of a maritime force. Now, had we shown that -- gone public with that document, people wouldn't have fought, because people who were sincerely anti-fascist and were against the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina is today a subservient class in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm honoured to be a member of that class.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's time to take a break. After the break, I have some more questions in that area. But you mentioned Brac, which you said was where Mr. Izetbegovic's family was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you can put him the question a bit later because it's already 10 to 4.00. We shall have a break now and resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd just like to inform you that during the break I did some calculations, and I have 10 minutes from my own cross-examination, and from Mr. Coric, I have got 15, so I'll complete my cross-examination within that 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, when you spoke about Brac and Milanovac, could you explain to Their Honours where Brac is and where Mr. Izetbegovic's family was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brac is in the Republic of Croatia, and Gornji Milanovac and Donji Milanovac are in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think you have answered -- you have started to answer while Ms. Nozica was still asking questions. At least I was confused. I didn't know who was speaking. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brac, where Mr. Izetbegovic's family was, is in the Republic of Croatia, whereas Gornji and Donji Milanovac are towns in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at the Presidency meeting, and I'm referring to the second half time, the end of 1993, that is, did you indicate the bad move of attacking Vitez? And from the transcript, with the consultations held with the BH army already in August, 1993, that it was the planned target of the BH army. Do you remember that you discussed that issue?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. There were a number of times when I pointed this out, and I legitimately defended, because I would never have accepted sitting in a body which would legally attack areas inhabited by Croats. And when two Franciscan Friars were killed in Fojnica, then, at Izetbegovic's request, I went there to quell the hostilities. And I didn't know why Vitezit was so important to them, because I'm not a military expert, but the fact remains that the fighting went on quite intensely over there. And we, as the Presidency members, received information from the military structures of the BH army alone, and they said that those were the best guys, whereas those over there were not. But I would say this quite openly to Izetbegovic. I said that if there were to be a war between the Croats and Muslims, Bosniaks at the time, were it to grow into an all-out war between these two ethnic groups, it would be highly detrimental to both but it would be worse to the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let us take a look at what you did actually say at the Presidency meeting held on the 29th of December, 1993. And it is Exhibit 2D 00189. We see here -- well, the whole first page in Croatian. First tell us whether you remember the meeting.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Only the title has been translated into English, of that first page, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, on e-court may we have the page of which the number is 10/3, both in English and in the B/C/S. 10/3. It is 2D 04/0140. That's right. And can we have the corresponding page in English? In English, it is 2D 040143. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to read it from the beginning. It begins -- Mr. Ganic, who was the Presidency member; Mr. Komsic was also a Presidency member. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then we have you and Mr. Izetbegovic speaking. So this is what Ganic says: "At UNPROFOR, there are those who care about these conflicts. Don't forget that. Some foreign powers that care got involved there." And they are referring to Vitez throughout. Then Komsic says: "If people surrender their weapons, and if those who want to leave abroad do, then there are no problems." Izetbegovic says to that: "There is one thing there, that we don't get the factory in our possession." And then we come to the important point that you say, Kljuic says: "And our army cares about that. That is why we're not going to Foca but to Vitez instead. We are not kids either." Now, you clearly stated your position. Let's just tell Their Honours what Foca was at that period and why you reacted the way you did. What was the importance of Foca?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that it gives me great moral satisfaction to read this after so many years, because certain individuals from Zagreb and Herzegovina proclaimed me to be a traitor of the Croatian people who stayed in Sarajevo. They said that there were no Croats in Sarajevo. But all this is symbolic, expressed in symbols. Muslims were the most numerous in Foca, and in a way that was the symbol. This town was the symbol of trade, ability, and different types of skills. But, you see, the army, the BH army, was going to Vitez, not Foca, which meant this is the consequence of a process. And I have to tell you that the conflict between the Muslims and Croats is the most tragic portion of Bosnian history. When that conflict took place, at that point in time Milosevic and Karadzic questioned all military action on the eastern front and enabled the Muslims to be stronger on the western front, because they thought that if they took Travnik, Bugojno, Vitez and Fojnica, they won't ask for Grude, Foca, et cetera, Visegrad, and so on. So that was a terrible situation, and of course -- and perhaps the leadership, the military leadership, under the influence of Izetbegovic, thought that Travnik would be more important; Travnik, Bugojno, Fojnica, more important than Grude, Medzic [phoen] and Visegrad. However, when I said what I did, I expressed my disagreement. I said, "We're not children. We know what this would mean."
