And tried to prevent an escalation in the war with the Croats, because that would have been detrimental not only to the Croats, who, conditionally speaking, stayed on in territory where the Muslims were the majority, but Croats as a state-forming nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also for the Bosniak people, because it was the only link in the chain, that link which set up resistance to Serbian fascism.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I just want to go back to this for a minute. This is, in fact, why I asked you whether the Patriot League was formed, for example, in the territory of Foca from the beginning of 1991. Was there any information, according to which the Muslim leadership - that's what it was called at the time - preferred certain territories to others, although they kept, in fact, claiming that they were for a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not how I would interpret this. The Muslim people did resist Serbian fascism, but such operations were the product or the result of a situation. You must know that a lot of JNA officers joined the ABiH. They had been indoctrinated by the idea that Croats were Ustashas. And this could be seen with Halilovic. Zagreb and Belgrade were the same enemy. Initially they only mentioned Zagreb but then they added Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kljuic, my time is short, so -- my question wasn't about the Muslim people. I'm referring to what was the product of the political and military leadership. It didn't concern the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my personal misfortune and misfortune of the Croatian and Bosnian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina was that President Izetbegovic and President Tudjman didn't like each other. They didn't tolerate each other, and the result was that two ethnic groups suffered. Secondly, there were public manifestations. There were a number of secret agreements, some of which we are unaware of. Some have been transcribed; some haven't. But since I knew both of them, I had close personal contact with both of them, and in the end neither of them had much fondness for me, but since I did know them, they enjoyed betraying people. In fact, they betrayed their own people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. I admit that what you are saying is quite interesting, but I'm running out of time, so let's go back to this Presidency session. Do you remember having intervened at this Presidency session with regard to the ties between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Islam countries? And you tried to inform the Presidency of contacts with Egypt. It's the same document, 2D 00189, page 4/3, both in the English and in the Croatian version. 4/3. That's the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the English version. Can we have the Croatian version? It starts at the top. Mr. Kljuic is speaking. It's the same page. Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll now read it out. You say: "Can I express my own opinion?" And do you agree that you're addressing Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "Are you going to express support for Egypt as one of our pillars in the Islamic world? I have made a suggestion, and in my assessment, in the case of Turkey, everything is fine. As far as Egypt is concerned, we should subsequently submit a request to the ministry. In other words, we should not issue an order. We should talk perhaps even to the Minister of Foreign Affairs to put the emphasis on Egypt, because I feel that Egypt could assist us significantly in a political sense." And this is what Mr. Izetbegovic said in reply: "I believe that Egypt could help us. However, what is at stake is how much influence it has in the Muslim and in the Western world. At the moment, Saudi Arabia has the most influence in the Western world. Given the financial situation, Egypt is an economically dependent country. If someone in the West is independent here, well, all this depends on Saudi Arabia because of oil, because of the sacred grounds there, and because of the fact that their revenue amounts to $200 billion over there. So Saudi Arabia is a country whose voice is most heard over there, and they are listened to the most. A few months ago they curtailed British government action, and they threatened they were going to put an end to important acquisitions, et cetera. Egypt cannot act in this way. I'm not sure that Egypt is a very influential country. As far as influence in the Muslim world itself goes, as far as its influence in the Muslim world itself goes, Egypt is not the country that has the most influence either. It's not because of the peace problems it has with Israel, et cetera. It is not the most influential country. There are two countries there which have a lot of influence; Saudi Arabia on the one hand, Iran on the other, for certain countries that are more rigid, and Pakistan, a country which has balanced politics. Contacts should be established with Egypt." You continue to insist on Egypt. That's consistent with the policies you have mentioned here before the Chamber. And my question is now as follows: When this was happening on the 20th of December, 1993, were there any citizens of Serbian or Croatian nationality who were still in Sarajevo and who would have believed this to be in their own interest? They would have believed that close contact should be established with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Iran, rather than with countries such as Turkey and Egypt, which are the countries that you preferred.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally they wouldn't have advocated such a position at the time, nor would they have advocated -- nor would they advocate such a position today. I'm a politically mature individual, and because of Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the Secretary-General of the UN, and because of Egypt's influence in the intellectual world in Muslim countries and in Turkey, because Turkey is a secular country, well, because of these factors, we believe that we should establish relationships with them, if relationships were to be established with anyone. I didn't want to use religion to introduce Shia Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, et cetera. But finally, when the situation was very dangerous for our country, five Presidency members in Bosnia and Herzegovina issued reports of their own against the instrumentalisation of religion in the army, against using religion in the army. I was the chief of the delegation of the Presidency of Serbs and Croats. We were received by Anthony Lake, the Chief of the Security of the USA. We were being prepared for the Dayton Agreement. And we discussed these matters - this was in 1995 - the condition sine qua non for Bosnia-Herzegovina as a secular state, so Turkey was to be a model for us. Turkey, out of all the Muslim countries, was a model. However, religion was instrumentalised by all three sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the results of the most recent elections demonstrate this. When we would talk about the Croats, we can see the role that the church played in its tragedies, et cetera. So in a multinational country, you have a fourth confession. You have the Jewish faith. The Jews are not numerous but they have much influence in Sarajevo. So in that country, where you have four monotheistic religions, the only way to survive is to have a secular state. However, no one was in favour of a secular state, because for the sake of elections, for the sake of one's political future, religion can play a vital role.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljuic. I regret not having had sufficient time to discuss a subject that has often been brought up in the course of your testimony, that of an indivisible Bosnia and Herzegovina. I had some questions about that. I also didn't have time to ask you about the most recent elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But I have now completed my cross-examination. Thank you very much. And I will now give the floor to my colleagues. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Counsel. Now for the next Defence team. Who will be taking the floor on behalf of Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak will be asking the questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please put technical questions to this witness. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will restrict myself to technical questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljuic, I can't talk to you in general terms; I'm not allowed to do so. And given the fact that we have limited time, and since you're one of the crucial witnesses in this case, if I ask you about certain documents, can you tell me very briefly whether you are familiar with the document or not so that we can move on quickly. This is only because time is limited.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We both share the same desire.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to go back to the agreement between Boban and Karadzic of the 6th of May, 1992. Can we see 3D 000430. That's the agreement in question. Can we read through item 5 of the agreement. I'll just read out item 5. "By this agreement we no longer have reasons to curtail the conference of the European Union on Bosnia-Herzegovina. Both parties want the conference to continue urgently." That's item 5. Is that correct, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not familiar with the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You have it here.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that Mate Boban didn't have the power to negotiate with the Serbs. He was only one of 44 representatives of mine in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, look, I understand what you're saying, but I don't have enough time. Please just have a look at the item and say whether that's what it actually says. We've already discussed what Mate Boban's role was. Is item 5 what I said it was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read it out correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the name "Franjo Boras"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Franjo Boras was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was a Croat. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was legally elected.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in his book, "The Bosnian and Herzegovinian Chaos," in 1996 -- 3D 00446 is the number of this document. Could we please have it on the screen. In that book of his, he described how Cutileiro and Lord Carrington asked them and him personally to go and talk to the Serbs. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can we see page 244. Can we see the following page, please, and then everything will be in order. The following page, please. These are the titles of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: He says, towards the end of our conversation with the Croatian delegation, Lord Carrington said the following: "Mr. Boras, if you don't reach an agreement, we'll let you kill each other and then we will impose our own solution on you." Mr. Boras answered: "Lord Carrington, how should we agree on anything, and with whom? The Serbian aggressor has everything at his disposal. He has all the military equipment of the JNA. You can hear the noise of the mortars and large guns from the surrounding hills. When we talk to them, it falls on deaf ears. The representatives of the Muslim people are passive. They don't do anything to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they are still hoping that the Yugoslav People's Army will provide assistance." And then two lines below, towards the end of the conversation: "Cutileiro informed us that all three delegations should reach an agreement about the territorial boundaries of the three constitutive units within Bosnia and Herzegovina without the presence of the international community." And then it says: "With regard to the conclusions in Sarajevo, on the 6th of May, 1992, a meeting was held in Grac between the Croatian and Serbian delegations. The Croatian delegation was headed by Mate Boban. Vlado Santic and I were also members of the delegation." So, according to Mr. Boras, a legally elected member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he was also a member of that delegation, and they had discussions there. Is that what it says in the book?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't read the book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But you have it here in front of you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me assist you. Wait a minute. Franjo Boras had been legally elected, but he didn't have the power to negotiate without consulting the president of his party. He didn't have the power to negotiate with the Serbian side. On the other hand, at that time it was only Milosevic who had acted against us in Croatia and in Bosnia. And Franjo Boras had also taken an oath, according to which he would protect the territorial integrity and the freedom of a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina. By negotiating with them, he violated the oath he had taken.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to see or to establish what has been written in this book. I like you and there are many things that we could agree on. But could we just agree on what Franjo Boras wrote down? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we move into private session, very briefly, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why do you want to go into private session? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Because there is something that I would like to say that I believe should not be said in open session. It has to do with Franjo Boras.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'd like to clarify something with regard to the consequences of the meeting in Grac. Josip Manolic, a witness, testified before this Chamber that, after the meeting in Grac, hostilities between the Croats and Muslims -- sorry, Serbs ceased. Please have a look at the map you have in front of you. My question is as follows: After the 6th of May and the so-called agreement on division, did the following events take place: First of all, in Bosnian Posavina, from May until June, did the army of Republika Srpska, after intensive fighting with the HVO, take over Derventa, Modrica, and Bosanski Samac? You can see that on the map. You can see the lines of attack of the Serbian army on Bosnian Posavina. Did this take place in 1992, from May to October, up until Bosanski Brod fell?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But can't you see how absurd that agreement is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, this is what I'm discussing, this is what I'm talking about. Did you know that the army of Republika Srpska launched an attack on Livno on the 23rd of -- from the 23rd to the 25th of May, 1992? They wanted to break through Livno and get to Split.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. I don't know the details, but I remember the operation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know that after that meeting, the Republika Srpska army broke through to the Neretva River, took the municipality of Stolac, most of the municipality of Capljina, and the eastern part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that in mid-June, 1992, HVO forces, with some assistance from the ABiH that wasn't fully fledged at the time, liberated Stolac, Capljina, et cetera, those territories?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Jajce fell after heavy combat on the 29th of September, 1992, and the army of Republika Srpska drove back the forces of the HVO and the ABiH and took the town and municipality of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there was no heavy fighting, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. We'll discuss that later. Do you know that during 1993, continuously with varying intensity, there were artillery attacks by the Serb army on the Mostar-Stolac area?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That the army of Republika Srpska attacked the municipalities of Tomislavgrad, Livno, Tomislavgrad and Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That the army of Serbia attacked Orasje, Posavina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a daily basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And the HVO units -- and the HVO units were defending Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, Bihac, Usora, Zepce, Vares, Gradacac, Brcko, Tuzla, those areas. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the map we see 11 HVO brigades and one HVO battalion which were established and were located outside what we later referred to as the provinces of -- provinces 3, 8, and 10, which were in provinces 1, 5, and 9, in actual fact. Are you aware of that? Do you know about those brigades?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You were referring to the provinces according to the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Now, would you agree with me that all those 11 brigades and the HVO battalion that was there, that they were established and that they fought on the territory which was outside what is mentioned here as the banovina of Croatia within Bosnia-Herzegovina? Take a look at the map, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I helped one of the Defence counsel explain what "banovina" meant last time. Banovina is not fact; it is fiction. On the other hand, everything you say is quite correct as far as the fighting was concerned, that the Croats made their contribution to the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. (redacted) If, after his agreement, everything went counter to it. And the second point is that we in the Presidency reached a decision to form armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which meant that all those defending Bosnia-Herzegovina - and that was the greatest problem I personally faced - was how to incorporate the HVO and the BH army and HOS at that point in time. Now, the problem arose with the behaviour of the different commanders. Now, this contribution by Croatia to the defence of BH was very important and indubitable. It was much more than just being an active defence. It was helping logistics in the different regions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, logistical support for Gradacac and Tuzla, for example, where the commander of the 2nd BH army corps was located and that was Zeljko Knez; and the town of Gradacac, Mejacevic. So you're just pointing out the positive features which we can accept. However, the conflicts arose on an interpersonal level, political level, outside the system and the institutions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, there's no doubt about that. We're not challenging that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there's a mistake in the transcript. In line 13 of that same page, it wasn't the contribution of Croatia but the Croatian people. That's what the witness said. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, it's just because of the time constraints that I can't enter into those -- into a debate of that kind and we can't go into the details. Otherwise, rest assured that I'd be happy to clear up the interpersonal relations and how many commanders of the BH army had previously been in the Yugoslav army during the aggression against Croatia. There are a lot of details of that kind. But I'd like to ask you to restrict yourself to certain facts, that there were 11 brigades fighting for Bosnia-Herzegovina outside areas which we, here, conditionally refer to as "banovina"; is that right? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May we move on to the next exhibit. 3D 00431 is the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, while we're waiting for the document, look at the red lines on the map, please. After the fall of Jajce, was it the intention of the army of Republika Srpska to break through to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they kept laying siege to Sarajevo but they weren't very good soldiers and didn't succeed in taking control of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I don't mind about Sarajevo. That's not the point. But to try and break through the corridor up to Jajce and Travan. Now, look at the Bosanska-Posavina corridor on the map now, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, I will slow down. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, it may be good to identify the map with a number, and it would also be good, when Mr. Praljak -- General Praljak is referring to the map and lines, to sort of have the witness exactly point to the particular map so we can get it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in a similar fashion, Your Honour, it would also be helpful if specific dates were used. We're generally skipping around continually from 1990 to 1994 and 1995. Could we also have Mr. Praljak give the specific dates of the questions he puts to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, bear that in mind, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The exact dates of the individual operations, and I state them, I give the months and dates: Jajce, Posavina, Livno, all this is in 1992. And you have that enumerated, the exact dates when what happened after the meeting in Grac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, sir, point to the corridor that the Serbs were defending on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can get up and show you. This was the corridor which linked Banja Luka to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have finished with the map. But would you now take a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. [Interpretation] May we have a number assigned to the map, an IC number, so that we can refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar, a number, please, for the map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit IC 47, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I've been told, Mr. Kljuic, that your answer wasn't included, your answer to my question, whether the army of Republika Srpska wanted after fall --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down and repeat what he's saying. It's impossible to translate at this speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that they weren't very good soldiers and you had to have a bit of -- some high morals and so on, enthusiasm, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, again we would like to ask you - and the interpreters further ask you - to slow down and wait until Mr. Praljak finishes with his question, and only after please kindly respond to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. It is not my intention to speak fast. I'll do my best to slow down. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, take a look at what -- something else you have in front of you. I have a video about the events in Polog where you were yourself. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In Polog, near Mostar, towards Siroki Brijeg, the Croatian people stopped a Yugoslav People's Army tank column; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we get a date, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 7th to the 9th of May, 1991. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's what I was just going to say, but thank you for giving me the date. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic arrived and you yourself arrived. Now, is it true that the Croatian people met you with acclamation? There was great applause when you arrived with Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived on the 7th, in the morning, and Izetbegovic arrived in the afternoon of the 9th, and we were greeted, although among those present there were those who wanted incidents to break out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true. But on the footage you saw, you were welcomed with acclamation and applause; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then, at Izetbegovic's request, this tank brigade was left to move toward Kupres, was allowed to move toward Kupres.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 72 hours of a great deal of trial and tribulation on my side. I was arrested together with General Jerko Doko, the minister, by General Andzelic, whose son in Sarajevo was propagating brotherhood and unity. Furthermore, President Tudjman and the late Cardinal Kuharic, the famous cardinal, also made recommendations that they be let through. I consulted them because I was faced with a difficult situation. Now, can you imagine that for the first time after World War II, in socialist Yugoslavia, a column of 168 tanks in full military combat was stopped? We have to look at the period we're talking about. In Croatia only two incidents had broken out at that time. The aggression had not escalated to Croatia yet. And there were many of those both in the field and in Zagreb who thought perhaps that it was better that the war, the terrible war, begin there. And I have to tell you, not only because of my own capabilities and for my own sake but because of some of the people that helped me there, and one of them was Slobodan Bozic - I always like to emphasise that - and another point is this: Colonel Pantelic, the commander of the Mostar corps -- it was a very difficult time. For 72 hours I didn't sleep at all. There were provocations all the time. And I said, "Colonel Bogdan," I think was his name, "you and I are faced with a very difficult situation here, but we can only pull out of it if you don't fire, if you don't shoot, and I'll do all the rest." So you had all this force coming from Belgrade, from where General Spirkovski was the commander of the 1st Army zone, giving directives that the army must go through at 1400 hours. How could it pass across all the people? So the Croatian people did, indeed, do that. It was a symbol of resistance. It was the first time in communist Europe that a squadron of that kind of the 4th Conventional Army was stopped. That was the first example of anything like that, any military might being stopped like that by the people in the world.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I completely agree with you there. I'm not challenging that at all. But can we just note that that tank brigade, with that many tanks, later took part on the 9th and 10th of April, 1992, in fact, in the attack on Kupres, and one month later in the attack on Livno, that I mentioned, with the aim of moving to Split; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. Let me say I wasn't happy that they marched on Kupres.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. For goodness sake, nobody is claiming that. Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we prevented the massacre from the 7th to the 9th which had been envisaged for Polog. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Might the witness Mr. Kljuic be shown Exhibit 3D 00432 now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, it is the attack by the Krajina Serbs on the village of Unista, which is on Bosnian-Herzegovinian state territory. You are going to look at an aerial map. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, this is Ravno. That's not the right one. 43 -- 3D 0043 -- no, I don't seem to have the number. I seem to have mislaid it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the second page. The same document, next page. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can have it placed on the ELMO. Here we have it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes. Could we look and see the whole map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All I'm asking you is this: Do you know that on the 10th of May, 1991, the Krajina Serbs, under the command of Mile Martic, occupied the village of Unista, BH state territory, and expelled the Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we arrested Martic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have time to enter into a debate now, but you know that I would gladly discuss the response made by the authorities on an aggression like this. Would that be the beginning of war in any country?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, please. Then I'll ask you: How is it possible from the territory of the Republic of Croatia to attack Bosnia-Herzegovina? And you'll remain without an answer, you won't be able to answer. So don't ask me to answer that, that Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a state, should protect part of the territory being attacked by a paramilitary formation from another state when that particular state does not want to prevent that paramilitary formation from acting in another state.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you're absolutely right. The Serbs occupied part of the territory of the Republic of Croatia and Croatia was not able to prevent that from happening. So I completely agree with you on that score. Now, all I'm asking you is this: An occupation of part of state territory in every country would be -- would denote the beginning of a war against that country.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it would, but Croatia was unable to prevent it and defend it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm talking about interpretation, not what actually happened. I'm only talking about what the interpretation theoretically was, what the political structures theoretically thought, whether they took this to be the start of an aggression.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May we have 3D 00432 now, please. 3D 00432.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, it's the same question. Ravno, we're referring to Ravno, and my question is a simple one. Did the Serbs, the army of Republika Srpska in fact, attack the village of Ravno on the 15th of September, 1991 and on the 6th of October, 1991, and expel and kill the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May we now have the following document: Exhibit 3D 00445.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Their Honours have received a complete translation of the Islamic declaration written by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have you read the Islamic declaration?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then there's no need for me to ask you whether the political message from the Islamic declaration is a secular civic Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the Muslims to be 50 per cent, and then to move to an Islamic republic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a theoretical book, a theoretical work. It could be called a utopian work, like Saint Simon or John Locke, and so on, along those lines, because no mention is made of any names in it or states in it. But it is a theoretical possibility and discussed on a theoretical level, of how the Muslim would act in a state in which they were in the majority, what their conduct in such a state would be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At the time of the first parliamentarian elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was the Islamic declaration printed in over 200.000 copies and distributed to the Muslim population, mostly to members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all correct. But this text can't be understood by the majority of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In addition, I have to point out that at the time no one objected, not even the communists who were in power, nor other entities in Yugoslavia. No one took it very seriously. It had been printed and it was reprinted on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I understand you completely. Many books throughout history weren't taken very seriously, although they were precursors of certain events. However, there were 200.000 copies that were printed and these copies were distributed to the population. And they were distributed primarily to members of the SDA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, since they had so many copies, they had to distribute copies to members of the SDA. I think that even communist Muslims read the book. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we now see 3D 00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, as far as the Islamic declaration is concerned, it's a voluminous document. Which paragraph or page are you interested in? Which page or paragraph would you like to have admitted into evidence, since we're not going to admit the entire book into evidence? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've singled out the pages that I would like to be admitted into evidence, and in my opening speech, we had the translated versions. These pages we have in the Croatian version and in the English version. You've been provided with the entire bundle. The translation was obtained from Washington, from the Washington Library, and the parts that are to be entered into evidence concern number 16. There are other numbers I could find later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we'll do this subsequently, although we believe that the entire book should be admitted into evidence given the context, and the pages that are of particular interest should be marked. While we're waiting for the document to appear on the screen, on page 52, lines 21 to 23, the name of a witness from the Naletilic case was mentioned. Later we had a private session when this was done, so this should be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljuic, the book, "The Islamic Declaration," have you read the entire book from cover to cover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we now see 3D 00447 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: This is the text of the oath taken by members of the Patriotic League. My question is as follows: Was the Patriotic League established on the 17th of April or around the 17th of April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a minute ago I said I couldn't answer that question. This was done illegally, and you know that in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, when war is ended, then everyone tries to prove that they were active two years prior to the event and they request a certain pension on the basis of their activities. I don't know the exact date of its formation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know what sort of oath members of the Patriotic League would take?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'll show you the text of this oath. It's based on a book written by Nihad Halilbegovic, the facts on the Patriotic League in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo, 1994. On page 17 we have the relevant section: "I swear by Allah Jelleshanuhu that I shall always and at all times and in every place defend all interests of the Muslim people," et cetera. They then wanted to amend the oath, but unfortunately many documents have remained that refer to this text. I have certain other documents. Is it correct to say that the Patriotic League, which was the organisation at the time, addressed itself to the Muslim population and they had to swear by Allah?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you're referring to God, I don't think anything is unnatural there. Everyone could say, "may God help." How could we put this differently, invert this formulation? Is there some other people in Bosnia-Herzegovina that thought they would be defending the interests of some other people? That's quite natural. But there's nothing illegal here. Everyone defended their own interests at the beginning, initially. Fortunately, initially, the Croats and Muslims had common interests. Later, things developed differently. I regret the fact. But this text, the text of this oath, well, I'm not sure this is how it read. Do you know why? Because most of the people who joined the Patriotic League came from JNA units and they were atheists.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, all your explanations, on the whole, are correct; however, I'm saying that the text of the oath is as it reads here, according to this book written by a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I can also see what is written here. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. I can also confirm that in the HVO it doesn't say we swear by God, et cetera, but it always says that we will defend the Croatian people and other peoples. But we'll discuss that at greater length later on. I'll move on now. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can we now see 3D 00420.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: This document has been shown before this Court by Counsel Nika Pinter. It says that on the 27th of May, 1992, a decision was taken on forming Territorial Defence units. This decision was signed by Alija Izetbegovic, as can be seen on the third page, page 3. We've already seen the document; it's already been shown. Have a look at the first page, and could you tell us whether this is correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen the first page. Whose session is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we see who attended the session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was signed by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this document. And these are the names of people from one ethnic group, with the exception of one person.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. The witness said that Mate Sarlija was a Muslim. When we read this out, we have the name Nijaz Batlak. But when you read out all these names, is there a single Croatian name you can find?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's see the second page. Have a look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I look at the names, not a single one, unless someone felt he was a Croat by nationality, and I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's see page 1.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this was just a Presidency memorandum. It's not a Presidency document. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at page 3, please. Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is this Mr. Izetbegovic's signature? And is this the relevant stamp, which is not very visible?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And we have the protocol number there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there's a slight error in the transcript. It doesn't fully reflect the witness's answer. Page 69, line 3. The witness said that it is Izetbegovic's private document. He said something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. I was never familiar with this, and I wouldn't have signed it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You believe this is Izetbegovic's private document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he signed it, and we have a state stamp and it says, "Memorandum of the Presidency." But these decisions weren't the subject of a discussion at any Presidency session that I attended. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Please, could you put the chart on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While you are looking at it, may I ask a question with regard to this list. To some extent at least, but I cannot identify it completely, it refers to different localities. It seems to be geographically based in some way. And I wonder whether the localities with a Croat majority are included in this, or whether this only covers troops that are assigned or created in places with a Muslim majority; Livno, the municipalities along the Croatian border, for instance. Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Everywhere, apart from the territory that was under the control of the Serbs. The other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to this text, was under Muslims and one Serb. There wasn't a single Croat. This is what the witness has testified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Stop, please. I said that's what this document says. However, the document isn't valid. It doesn't reflect the actual situation on the ground. At the time -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This piece of paper is not a valid document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I know that your role in the Presidency has perhaps been omitted, but this piece of paper is, in fact, a decision signed by Mr. Izetbegovic in his capacity as the President of the Presidency. He issues an order. This document is a valid one. Although you don't believe that this document should be valid, that's a different matter. It doesn't reflect the situation in accordance with the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that case, I understand you fully.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, you don't understand me. This document is not real. It was perhaps drafted, compiled. But when independence was obtained, since Bosnia and Herzegovina had a Territorial Defence force but the Serbs had taken the weapons and supplies away, well, the Territorial Defence remained in place. And I have to mention the names of the individuals who were active in Bosnia and Herzegovina's Territorial Defence. Later on, these were local functionaries. There was an institution in the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, please assist me. I'd like to discuss matters with you at length, but the Chamber hasn't given me enough time or limits me to technical questions.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I want to assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please just tell me whether you are familiar with this document or not.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a valid document, because at that time there was an official Territorial Defence force of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the command of the Ministry of Defence. That was also composed of generals. There was Siber and Divjak, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, and many others. And this shows that these percentages are here simply not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may intervene at this point. First, there was a question by Judge Trechsel which has not been answered, and I think it deserves to be answered. Unfortunately, Mr. Kljuic decided to start answering questions which weren't posed to him. So would I ask him to just please -- perhaps the question can be posed again so General Praljak could answer that question for the record. Secondly, the word "valid" is being used. I'm wondering whether it's "valid" versus "legal". Is this a legal document, or is it a legal document or a legal decision versus valid? And I think perhaps Mr. Kljuic is thinking that this is not a legal -- that the document is not legal or that the decision is not legal, which would mean that the president - and that's his signature with the seal - would have created an illegal document; in other words, acting outside his constitutional powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljuic, you said that the document was not valid. What does this mean exactly? Does it mean that the document doesn't reflect the actual situation on the ground, or this document that is signed by Mr. Izetbegovic is in some way illegal? Please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both. There was a Territorial Defence force and its structure was quite different from the structure mentioned here. It was a legal body. And secondly, the president of the Presidency, or the presiding individual, the chairman of the Presidency, let's say, not the president of the Presidency, couldn't appoint individuals to subordinate military positions. The commander of the Territorial Defence had that role. So this shows that this is an illegal document. And the fact that it says "Memorandum from the Presidency" and it bears the Presidency stamp, well, this is an abuse of his power. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: This is what I'm trying to demonstrate, too, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I confirmed. You said that this was the only document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. I just asked you whether you were familiar with this document, whether it had been signed by Alija Izetbegovic and whether what it says is, in fact, what it says.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't check the protocol. Who knows whether that protocol number is the right number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now have a look at the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, no. My question now comes, and only as a footnote. This is a document the witness says he has never seen. He has no relation to it. So I think if the Prosecution were to present it, the valid lawyers of the Defence would immediately jump up and say, "This is not admissible." And I wonder whether the same should not apply the other way around. Oh, they are jumping now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm jumping. The gentleman is saying -- if I -- the gentleman is saying as follows: That President Izetbegovic was acting outside his constitutional powers at the time that he created this document, and he's making these appointments. And what it shows is that you have a double-faced policy; one that is open, where he is acting within his constitutional powers as the president of the Presidency, and here where he surreptitiously is acting on his own because he happens to be the president of the Presidency. And I think that's what the gentleman is trying to say; that this is an illegal document per se; in other words -- and so de facto you can see Izetbegovic acting now outside his constitutional powers. And this is while he -- and this gentleman here, at the same time when this document was generated, was a member of the Presidency, which begs the question: If he's a member of the Presidency, how dare the president of the Presidency surreptitiously make these nominations? And I think that's the point that General Praljak is making. And to tie it in with your very valid question was: Are these locations simply controlled by Muslim majorities or other places? And I think that's why your question, on which I insisted on getting an answer, would be most important, because from there we could see, perhaps for one moment, where the president of the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic, is going with this surreptitious document, which is, you know, outside the constitution -- his constitutional powers. And I think that's what the gentleman is trying to say, so -- I'm just trying to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- I did not doubt what the witness has said. I understood it exactly the way you have repeated it. That was not the issue. The issue was to the document, but I said it was a footnote. The question that General Praljak has not answered, I will put it more precisely. Could you please, in this list, point out the nominations of -- or the creation of troops which are destined to be engaged in Grude and Livno? Well, Mr. Petkovic may answer if he knows better. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, he doesn't know better, but -- no. That refers to the majority Muslim population. He did not do this for Grude where it was the Croatians who were in the majority but just for the areas which he considered were inhabited by a majority Muslim population. I'd now like to ask page 3 of that document to be placed on the ELMO, because part of the document was not photocopied, it was left out. So I'd like to show Mr. Kljuic, because there's an additional text written in Izetbegovic's hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I listened to the French translation until now, and now I would like to ask a question before Mr. Scott will have, finally, his say. My question is the following: That Mr. Kljuic, a few minutes ago, mentioned this document and he said that it was a memorandum, and my question is that -- I ask mainly those who are -- who are using the Croat or -- Croat, Serbian or Bosnian language, that when we see here in the preamble of that paper or document it says that -- actually, it says the name of the Presidency, in English, "Issues the following decision"; in Croatian, "Donosi odluku o formiranju jedinica teritorijalne obrane." So now my question is if it is really a decision, as it was translated into English, or a memorandum, as it was said -- it was mentioned by Mr. Kljuic. So that is my question to Mr. Praljak or those who would like to answer the question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Decision.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] It's a decision. He decides. He is deciding. The decision is final, clear, and precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, just two words of explanation for the term "memorandum." As the witness used it, it is the usual way for using this concept which denotes a piece of paper which, in the upper left-hand corner, has the person who has issued it. It says it's a document of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or whatever. That's what we mean by "memorandum". That letterhead, in fact. It's an empty piece of paper with that letterhead, a blank piece of paper with the letterhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid all misunderstanding, it would be "header" in the English, "header". And we refer to "header" or "letterhead" as "memorandum" in our language, as the official paper, note paper used by an institution for writing whatever it has to write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Several points to be made. First, to follow up on Judge Trechsel's comments a few minutes ago. I couldn't agree more. That's, frankly, been happening all afternoon. The witness has been shown a series of documents that the witness has no personal knowledge of. I haven't objected because, in the past, that seems to be sometimes a separate procedure and I just didn't want to be on my feet. But I think it's been happening all afternoon. We have put documents in front of the witness the witness has no knowledge of. Secondly, I don't think counsel should stand up and characterise the witness's testimony. It's not up to counsel to get up and say, "I think this is what the witness is saying." Those remarks are better saved for closing argument. Number 3, it's also not up to Mr. Praljak or Mr. Petkovic or any of the accused to stand up from their chair and give evidence. If they want to give evidence in this case, they can take the witness stand right here and I'll be happy to cross-examine them. It is not up to them to give evidence in this case from their chairs. And that's what's been happening again this afternoon, as it has before. Number four, I don't understand the relevance of any of this. We've spend all -- most of the afternoon on irrelevant matters. I don't understand the relevance of this last 25 minutes or so. How is any of this a defence to the expulsion of Muslim civilians in Mostar in June 1993 and thereafter? I don't understand the relevance of any of this. And finally, Your Honour, I would like to inquire about time. I don't know how the Defence allocated time among themselves. Mr. Praljak has now been going at least for 50 minutes. I would like time for redirect, and I do not know what how much time is left for the Defence combined. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consider that it is logical for the Prosecutor at this point in time to have got up on his feet to intervene and to explain the opinions of Mr. Trechsel. However, I have to say, not because he mentioned me but because I think it is a matter of principle, what Judge Prandler has just said, on page 1 here it says on this document that it was the Presidency who -- when I saw the first page; I don't see it now. That it was in May 1992 that this was compiled by the Presidency. Mr. Stjepan Kljuic at that time was a member of the Presidency, and he had to have attended this meeting or the following meeting when the minutes were adopted. So Mr. Kljuic should have known about this document. And there is no better suited person, better placed person, to tell us whether this document was adopted at the Presidency meeting or not. Your Honours, just finally, I'd like to add one more sentence and that is this: That the examination conducted this afternoon was done with the best knowledge of the indictment, so I'm surprised at the Prosecutor's remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we go back to page 1. The header of the document clearly states who issued the document, and those are indisputable facts. I don't want to respond to what the Prosecutor has just said because I'm taking up my client's time. But I think, in light of all this, that is quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kljuic, we've spent a lot of time on this document. This document is entitled, "Decision on the Creation of Units for Territorial Defence." The stamp and the signature there indicate that it is the president of the Presidency who has signed this document. In the preamble of the document, which is based on article 41 which has to do with those texts governing the armed forces, in the preamble, a reference is made to a meeting which was held on the 27th of May. That said, this document is dated the 27th of May. So we can reasonably conclude that the Presidency met on the 27th of May, and the president of the Presidency has signed this decision. Were you there? Did you attend the Presidency meeting? It's either a "yes" or a "no" answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Sarajevo. There was nowhere else that I could have been but at the Presidency meeting, because during the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina I lived in the Presidency building. So I was in the building itself, on the premises. However, I do not remember that I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you remember a meeting during which Mr. Izetbegovic had said that territorial units needed to be created, as can be read in this decision? Do you remember this at all, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, in looking at the list of those appointed, many of them were heads of certain groups which defended, more or less successfully, the country. Now, they had to be incorporated into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a non-response to your direct question. Your direct question was extremely precise and it deserves to be answered by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, indeed. As a rule, my questions are usually pretty accurate. So my question runs as follows: Did you hear about, or did you hear anything about at one point in time, at the level of the Presidency, that the Territorial Defence units needed to be set up, as can be seen here? And these had to be deployed in Zenica, Sarajevo, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did our best to establish such units, but I would never have agreed to these names, nor was I at the meeting when this was put forward, if it was put forward at the meeting. Perhaps it was written outside the meeting, outside the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that case, a last question. You have answered my question, but I want this to be on the record. Did the president of the Presidency have the authority to decide on the creation of Territorial Defence units? I think you said no; I think you said that that was not part of his duties. So what is your definitive answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My definitive answer is this: That we had a Territorial Defence which was active from the first day of the aggression, and that for the appointment of the lower-ranking commanders, it was the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence that was responsible, not the presiding officer of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And who at the time was head of the Territorial Defence Main Staff, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do remember. First of all, there was a gentleman, a JNA colonel, his name was Efendic. Izetbegovic wasn't very fond of him, and then he replaced him later on and brought in Sefer Halilovic, and then he replaced Sefer Halilovic as well, ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The document, perhaps a number of people have overlooked this, but I don't think so, the Minister of Defence, according to the last paragraph, has played a particular role who needs to organise the command structure of the units. Who was Minister of Defence at the time, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jerko Doko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you don't remember whether Mr. Jerko Doko talked to you about his duties, the fact that he needed to set these units up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do remember. We were together every day. It was wartime. We would be in the same building the whole day. All these guys who had patriotic feelings but did not have the education, and some of them before the war were even delinquents, they had to be established into a system of some kind, a territorial defence. And they needed help and assistance. And it was, in fact, how the BH army was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we have the break - after the break we'll only have one hour - this was the last question put by Mr. Scott: Mr. Praljak, what is the relevance of all of this? Because what is it you want to establish on the basis of this document? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The foundation of the indictment is the joint criminal enterprise, which is based on premises, the premises that the Croatian leadership and these six men sitting here in 1992 and in 1993 as well, as well as in 1994, worked exclusively to separate a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that the Muslims were those who were in favour of an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina; that we were separatists, and that our philosophical thought was to look at war and the fate of the Croatian people, how we viewed this, and that caused all the evils and crimes that took place on that territory from that point in time onwards. Now, since the documents which I am presenting here quite obviously show, together with the maps and the brigades and the facts of how Mr. Izetbegovic behaved, the Patriotic League behaved and the territorial units behaved, the number of Croats - and there were zero on this list, zero Croats on this list - that that fact in the indictment has nothing to do with the truth as it stands. And showing documents of this kind leads to nervousness and anxiety on the part of the Prosecutor, because none of the groundwork of the indictment which they wish to impose can, in my deep conviction, be proved with these documents. So I feel that these documents are relevant for the Court. They show the development of events on a long-term basis, from day to day over a longer period of time, how the situation deteriorated, how the war came about, and then how, as a consequence of that war, as a consequence of the impossibility of controlling people within that war, arrive at the facts that we're discussing. That is why I believe, Your Honours, that what I'm saying is grounded in the indictment itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that, as far as you're concerned, this document is relevant because there is a connection with your defence strategy. It is now nearly a quarter to 6.00. The registrar has just told me that a name has to be deleted on the record, so we can only resume at ten past 6.00. It has to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another 45 minutes. Mr. Scott, how much time would you need for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would have liked to have something like approximately 20 minutes, but I'll settle for whatever the Chamber can give me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to inform you that my client has one hour and 15 minutes; 30 minutes were granted to him by the accused Petkovic and 50 minutes by the accused Coric. That amounts to an hour and a quarter. He has taken up 45 minutes so far, according to the registrar, so he has another half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have another half an hour, and then the remaining 15 minutes will be granted to Mr. Scott. So please don't waste any time. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, please have a look at the document on the ELMO. You can see that, in addition to the document on the Territorial Defence, there is something that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic wrote; you can see the handwritten text. Can you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions about that. My next question concerns the arming of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the HVO from Croatia. Do you know that throughout the war weapons arrived from Croatia for the HVO and for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't arrive in Sarajevo for the HVO, not sufficiently. But everything else concerned agreements that were not institutional agreements. The SDA officials and Croatians, both high-ranking and low-ranking Croatians participated in this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a series of documents that I would like you to have a look at. Do you know who General Cermak was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. He was a quartermaster in the Croatian army for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that General Zagorac had that role, too?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's correct. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Please, can you show document 3D 00439.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, could you have a look at the date, the 7th of April. It says the 7th of April, 1993, and it says: "Permission to pass freely. The Main Staff of the HVO has approved a free pass, supplies being provided on the axis Grude-Srebrenica." And then it mentions three drivers, three Muslims. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was also an escort, also Muslims. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can we see 3D 00008. Could you enlarge the document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Zagreb, the 6th of March, the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. An order is concerned through the Grude logistics base. A certain amount of materiel and equipment has to be provided for Gradacac and Visoko. The drivers are all Muslims. It's addressed to the units -- it's for the units of the ABiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a Stipo Blazevic who is a Croat. One of the drivers is a Croat. But apart from that, everything that you have said is correct. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we see 3D 0009.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's the document. The Republic of Croatia, the Ministry of Defence. The 26th of March, 1993. Order for issuing materiel through the Grude logistics base. Seta Sajub from Sarajevo will take over the equipment, and apart from Franjo Juric to escort the convoy, all the others are Muslims. Do you know who Seta was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's his name?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sajub is his name, I think.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know a Seta who the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Later on. The 26th of March is the date, and this document states that, through the logistics base of Grude in Croatia, arms are being provided to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can we see 3D 00010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one very brief question that I'd like to put to you. I'm not going to take up a lot of Mr. Praljak's time. We have evidence that shows that the Republic of Croatia provided the ABiH with weapons in March, April, et cetera. The political authorities or those who lived in Sarajevo at the time, were they aware that, regardless of the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH, Croatia was delivering weapons to the ABiH? Was this something that they knew, or is this something that you just discovered now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Even when I wasn't a member of the Presidency, at the time I knew that, as far as Tuzla and Gradacac are concerned, weapons were delivered. This was done somewhat on a private basis and for strategic reasons. And I knew that Bosanska Krajina, including Bihac, was helped by Croatia. This can be interpreted in two ways. Firstly, they wanted to help the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina; but, secondly, if Bihac fell, the defence forces of Croatia would find themselves in a very difficult position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I add a question? Mr. Kljuic, have you seen any of these documents that have just been shown to you before? Have you seen these documents? Can you identify the documents? Can you say whether they are genuine, whether they are what they purport to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this took place outside of institutions. It concerned bilateral relationships between Mr. Tudjman and Izetbegovic with lower-level individuals. As to whether Croatia really delivered weapons selectively or not, I can't say. But I can confirm, on the basis of my own experience, that when I visited the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I also visited areas such as Tuzla, Vares, Gradacac; I was in the vicinity of Brcko, et cetera. And at that time, the high-ranking officials informed me of the fact that, in spite of all the misunderstandings, weapons did arrive or materiel did arrive in some parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'd just like to point out that the Court will be provided with thousands of such documents later on, not only a couple.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, if weapons from Croatia didn't get delivered to Bosnia and Herzegovina, how did the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina manage to open fire? Were weapons produced? How was it possible for weapons to arrive in any other way?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is very interesting, but since I'm also a victim of the relationships in force at the time, I'd like to put another question to you. How is it that you entered into a conflict when such friendly relationships existed? The greatest victim of that conflict are the Croats who remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina and primarily those who remained in large cities. If we had been asked for our opinion, such a conflict would never have broken out. However, later on, when certain other countries got involved - and you know whom Izetbegovic counted on - agreements were reached -- an agreement was reached that was well known, an agreement between Zagreb and Sarajevo. According to that agreement, assistance from Islamic countries would be delivered to Croatia, and on the basis of some sort of agreement, they would divide it. The Muslims received the larger part. However, this was all done privately. This was done outside of our institutions by bypassing institutions. I believe that they weren't able to neutralise the conflict between the Muslims and Croats until the Americans said stop, and then that's when the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established. That was on the 18th of March, 1994. That's the happiest day in my life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljuic. I would now like to go through some other facts, but how the war broke out is something that will be discussed for years. Have a look at this document dated the 26th of March, 1993. It says the 30th here, the 30th. "Seta from Sarajevo takes over delivery, and as far as the convoy escort is concerned, all those who made up the convoy were Muslims -- all those who made up the escort were Muslims." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I have another seven or eight documents that will be submitted to the Chamber. Let's skip this part now. It's no longer necessary to dwell on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you see this document? And do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. There's nothing that I can recognise here, but I can see the names of the drivers. I can see the sort of materiel that was delivered and I have no reason to doubt it, since I know that this was the main source of weapons, in addition to the source represented by the weapons that our units obtained when fighting the aggressor; or, in certain cases, they bought weapons in some other way. I have to say this because of the Judges: Bosnia-Herzegovina was a mini-Casablanca at the time. Everyone would come to sell weapons there. Certain soldiers from the international forces sold weapons. You know there were Ukrainians and Russians in Bosnia-Herzegovina, et cetera, et cetera. And since this was big business, that's how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we please scroll up. Have a look at the top of the document. We can see that it says, "The Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence." And can we see the signature and the stamp at the bottom. Could we scroll down now. Can we see the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which number? What's the number of the document? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Number 10, at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Zagorac, an advisor for the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. There are two other matters I'd like to address. Do you know about what is known as a historical agreement which Muhamed Filipovic represented on behalf of the Muslims? It was in Belgrade on the 2nd of August, 1991. Muhamed Filipovic, Radovan Karadzic. The date, the 2nd of August, 1991. Are you familiar with this historical agreement?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not only aware of it but I managed obstruct it. This was an act of betrayal of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because if such an historical agreement had been implemented, then only the Croats would not have been concerned by the agreement. They would have been the aggressors, et cetera, et cetera. However, when rejecting this agreement, I wouldn't have of much influence, in spite of the fact that I'm eloquent.
