I wouldn't have managed to have obstructed the agreement unless Mr. Izetbegovic had been against the agreement. And that is why I'm surprised. Why were Croatian policies against Izetbegovic at the time? Why was there such animosity? Let's be clear. You understand this, but I'm saying this for the sake of the Chamber. If Izetbegovic had accepted the agreement, the Serbs had the tanks and officers. If Izetbegovic had accepted this and if he had persuaded the Muslims, the Serbs would have mobilised 300.000 Muslims who would have crossed over or who would have gone to the west. They wouldn't have lingered on the Karlobag-Virovitica line. They would have gone as far as Rijeka probably. And that's a historical fact. And paradoxically, they came to a conflict between the Croats and Muslims later on because of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I know you want to explain everything to us, but let's see 3D 00281 on the screen, please. Can you just tell me whether this agreement existed; whether what it states is what I have said; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I can't answer the question like that, you know. Let me just say this: Belgrade tried to establish this agreement through Dobrica Cosic, and they wanted this agreement with the SDA. When this didn't function, they opted for a minority party. They brought in Zulfikarpasic, who was one of the candidates for the Presidency in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he obtained the least number of votes. He was number 42. Zulfikarpasic then went to Belgium.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, please, I'm talking about the text of the agreement that you can see before you. Was this text signed by Muhamed Filipovic and Radovan Karadzic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Let's see 3D 00433. It's a transcript of the programme shown on the federal television of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The academic Muharem Filipovic was a guest. His photograph has been presented to the Chamber. We can't have a look at it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But I'm drawing your attention to what's been underlined. I'll read it out: "As far as Bosnia is concerned, from the point of view concerning the Bosnian interests, concerning the interests of my people, we had to avoid war as matter of priority." He's talking about Bosnian people and about avoiding war. "That's why we were negotiating. I didn't invent this, neither did I negotiate to please myself, but the late Alija Izetbegovic shared my opinion, and therefore he gave me and Mr. Adil Zulfikarpasic the right to negotiate." Muhamed Filipovic said this on this programme. Have you seen this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I'll tell you how things actually happened. Mr. Zulfikarpasic and Muhamed Filipovic did go to Belgrade, but they informed Mr. Izetbegovic about the fact at the same time. I know about that. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is important. It will help you. Look, Izetbegovic didn't accept this, but being a practical politician, he let them go there to see how the Muslims would react. The Muslim politicians were against this, and that's why this historical agreement failed. But if it had succeeded --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, we've heard about that already, sir. But the fact remains that the agreement was attempted and we cannot discuss the perceptions and consequences this had on the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tragic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, tragic. Thank you. Tragic. Quite right. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Now, may we have this other document placed on the ELMO. It's an agreement -- the joint declaration signed by Momir Bulatovic, Alija Izetbegovic, Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic. The agreement or joint declaration was signed -- on the last page it says when. Let's look at the date. It's 1993 anyway. 1993, and the month is September.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: May we look at point 1 on the first page in the Croatian text. The Judges have the text in English. Let us look at point 1, and I'll read it out. "To do everything in our power for all hostilities to cease immediately and military conflicts between the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the forces of the Bosnian Serbs, pursuant an agreement of the 30th of July, 1993, that they cease immediately and by the 11th of September, 1993, at the latest, at exactly 1200 hours, and so establish a direct link or hot-line between military commanders in all areas." Is that what it says there, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but I'm not aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document was added to your list subsequently. I can see that you're looking for the document. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May we have the next page placed on the ELMO. Point number 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And I'm reading the document: "To establish a working group for special issues related to territorial delineation and separation between the two republics in the future union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the areas of Brcko, Bosanska Krajina, the Neretva river valley, Eastern Bosnia, and Mount Ozren, and also" - and I emphasise this - "to include the natural right of the two republics to have an exit to the sea, or approach to the sea." Is that what it says there, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does say what you've just read out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. So it doesn't say where this access to the sea will be.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there was a Boban-Izetbegovic agreement as well which determines where this access to the sea will be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please try and understand me.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you want me to accept a document that I am seeing for the first time. And when I want to help you and say where the access to the sea will be, you don't want to let me do that. There was a separate agreement between Izetbegovic and Boban.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll come to that in due course. I would be very happy to be able to discuss this for five days.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be that happy because it's going through all the troubles and tribulations that I went through. All I want to say is to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In this document, and I'm going to show you the last page in English, does it say what I read out?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you. I'm just saying that I haven't seen this before. I don't know. I'm not aware about this document. This is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That answer is quite all right. It satisfies me.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, good.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, let's see the last page in English with the signatories. Do you recognise the handwriting of Alija Izetbegovic and his signature?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A question, just to make absolutely sure. This document provides to be signed also by Momir Bulatovic and by Slobodan Milosevic, and these two have not signed; is that correct? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Momir Bulatovic and Slobodan Milosevic did not sign the document. It was signed by Radovan Karadzic, Alija Izetbegovic, David Owen, and Thorvald Stoltenberg.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, do you know that at that point in time, that is to say, during the summer months of 1993, an open, all-out offensive, Neretva '93 of the BH army towards areas inhabited by Croats where they were in the majority, with the aim of having access to the sea, as Sefer Halilovic publicly declared? Do you know about that? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me this, please: Do you know that, from the end of 1992 with the influx of the Mujahedin, and throughout 1993, the Muslim units, most of them, when they were being established and when they were going into battle would shout "Allahu Akbar"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instrumentalisation of religion in the army was a fateful thing for the army. But I have to tell you that all those Afro-Asian cadres who had arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not welcome for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, came in through Croatia and also the logistics centres that you mentioned as having sent weapons to, all of them. None of them went through via Milosevic's side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, correct, as well as weapons. But do you know that everyone, every single person, went via Croatia with permits from 250 humanitarian organisations registered in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now the question arises as to who allowed that many humanitarian organisations to be registered? Every country must control the work of foreigners, and I think that Croatia knew at the time what those people were doing, who later came to us and did what they did to us in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, a serious country, with a third of its territory occupied, with half a million Muslim refugees, with half a million or 300.000 Croatian refugees, with a new authority in power, with a new system, and the fact that any refusal to recognise any humanitarian organisation in Croatia would lead to revolt from the whole world saying that the Croats did not wish to allow humanitarian organisations to exist, tell me, please, was it possible to say that they would forbid the establishment of humanitarian organisations for assistance to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was that possible at all? Could they have been prohibited?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not have been prohibited but they could have been brought down to a reasonable number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, and it's my last question: Slavko Degoricija, who, through some of woman, sent you information what Franjo Tudjman wanted to do with you, what was he in the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the first Croatian government, and he was the reconstruction minister, which was an important post in view of the fact that Croatia was an occupied country in part, that it had been destroyed, that an end of the war was expected and reconstruction and development follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Now, at that point during the war, the minister for reconstruction and development, you will agree with me, is a completely unimportant person in the government.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a personage and as and friend, I saw him as being someone very important, especially as he cautioned me through this woman. Now, as for his activities within the government, he was to leave it very soon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, that was your last question. That's what you said. You're not going to be asking more questions. And in addition, it's now a quarter to 7.00. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would like to tell the witness the following:

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Slavko Degoricija, he wasn't an advisor to President Tudjman or minister in any of the important ministries. How, then, could you have believed that this man was informing you, through a woman, of President Tudjman's intentions towards you? Could that have been just speculation or something that had no written traces anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just answer that question and that will be it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's very complicated, because my head was on the line both in Sarajevo and in other places. I was in danger. Now, later on, they eliminated me and brought in somebody else who later left Bosnia-Herzegovina, just like the prime minister that you mentioned earlier on. In the conflict between Izetbegovic and Tudjman -- and the people down there in Herzegovina listened to Zagreb because -- and I see in the context that Bosnia-Herzegovina was divided into three republics, that in Sarajevo there were no Croats. That's what was being said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Into two republics, sir.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this man Boban even said that the only people who stayed on were traitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over to you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just take a minutes of your time. The three documents that we saw on the ELMO, 3D numbers, we have them for future tendering into evidence. I would just like to mention the numbers, that they are 3D 00449, the first table of the Territorial Defence; the next is 3D 00450 and it is the decision with the handwritten passage by Alija Izetbegovic, the TO decision; and 3D 00451, that was the joint declaration, the last document we saw. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll deal with the tendering of documents tomorrow. Mr. Scott, it's your re-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we only have a few minutes. I will be very, very appreciative if you would try to keep your answers brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like the witness to please be shown Exhibit P 0060.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a -- you were asked several times about the policy of Izetbegovic and the Sarajevo government, about developments in the former Yugoslavia during this time, and about the alleged statement - and I say "alleged statement" because I think you addressed this in your earlier testimony, but we don't have time to get into this this afternoon - but in the alleged statement by Mr. Izetbegovic that this is "not our war." Can I ask you, please, to look at paragraph number 5 of this document, on the second page. Is it correct, sir, in the interests of time, if the record --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Just one moment, please. Please change me Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. If we could enlarge paragraph 5, please. I don't think we have the right reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. The right side. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct, in this record of this meeting of the HDZ BiH Presidency that both you and Mr. Kostroman signed, that a decision was taken at this meeting, as reflected here; that is, to endorse the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina of neutrality of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was the only possibility, that we don't take part actively in the aggression against Croatia and to paralyse Serbia and the JNA on the other hand, because it says here that Bosnia and Herzegovina mustn't be a training ground for attacks on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As of October of 1991, that was the official policy of the HDZ BiH. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've been asked various questions about why Bosnia-Herzegovina would allow the JNA to conduct operations against Croatia on its territory. Can you tell the Judges, very briefly, Mr. Kljuic, did anybody in Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time have the ability to prevent the JNA from operating anywhere in the former Yugoslavia, be it Croatia or Bosnia, if they chose to?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Yugoslav People's Army, according to the regulations of the time, had the right to conduct exercises, and by -- and the troop movement would always take place under the guise of exercises and training. On the other hand, Croatia did not have the possibility of preventing on its territory any JNA movement and shooting. I had a verbal duel with the then minister of defence who, at a meeting in Zagreb, once said, "Why are you shooting at us," claiming that there was shooting coming from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was true, but it was the Chetniks of the JNA doing the shooting. And I said, "Well, why don't you stop this Mirkovci place?" It's a Chetnik village near Osijek, 17 kilometres from Osijek, on the territory of Croatia. So the defence system of Croatia and the citizens defending Bosnia-Herzegovina could not stand up physically to the aggression and to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, by some point in 1991, was approximately one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia occupied by the JNA or Serb military forces?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Yugoslav People's Army and Serb insurgents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that President Tudjman had no greater ability than President Izetbegovic of Bosnia to prevent the JNA from doing what it wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not, no, because, as you saw earlier, the Croatian communists as well as the Bosnian and Herzegovinian communists betrayed their homeland and handed over the weapons of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me very briefly ask you, please, to next be shown Exhibit P 00116. And if I can direct and have the usher's assistance, please, to move as quickly as possible to what would be page 4 of the English version. I'm not sure -- I'm afraid I'm not sure in the B/C/S version, but maybe also page 4. Yes, thank you. If I could have you enlarge the paragraph on both pages that says: "The assessment of the work and role of the party ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the language where it says: "The attitude of the Croatian representatives in the BH Assembly, especially when the issue of the referendum was being decided, is a direct result of the absence of a clear political stance." Very quickly, sir, can you tell us, when it's described here, "the Croatian representatives in the BH Assembly," who is being referred to? And how do these people get to be the representatives in the BH Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had representatives on two bases. We had 44 representatives of the HDZ out of the 240 which the BH parliament had, the number of seats it had. Now, all our representatives, with the exception of one, were in favour of having a referendum on independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, sir, in the interests of time. These 44 representatives to the BH Assembly, were they, all of these representatives, elected or did they result from the 1999 -- 1990, excuse me, democratic election?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so, in fact, these democratically-elected Croats had favoured -- voted in the Assembly in favour of the original language of the referendum, as opposed to the Livno alternative language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You made several references during your testimony to Mr. Miro Lasic, and at one point when you were here before you were not given the opportunity to explain something further about the fact that he came to be involved in the Cutileiro talks and also then became a member of the Presidency in your place, if you will. Did you consider Mr. Lasic -- number one, I want to give you the opportunity to say whatever else you want to say about that before we finish; and number two, in that answer, if you could tell us, did you consider Mr. Lasic to be a moderate in the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first stage, until he replaced me, he was relatively moderate, but he was a man who was -- which all regimes could use. But he was not prone to violence. He was an intellectual, a member of the civic class, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Scott. I would like to have precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the answer to a question you have put before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It says, "the Croatian representatives." Are these representatives from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They're citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which were ethnic Croats --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because in parliament you had Muslims, Croats, atheists, Serbs, social democrats, reformists, liberals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was it the same Mr. Lasic who later left the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the time that you re-entered the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of, in fact, when all of the remaining senior Bosnian Croats had withdrawn from the central government prior to the time when you returned, if they had withdrawn --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question. It assumes a fact not in evidence. He's used the word "withdrawn." I want to point out that the Prosecution is not testifying. To use his own words, he can take the stand and I'll cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you aware, do you have any knowledge, Mr. Kljuic, about senior members -- Bosnian Croat members of the government withdrawing from the government; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some fled straight away when the aggression started, and they spent five months out of Bosnia. Of course, there were Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks there, but I'm referring to the Croats now. And they stayed on in Zagreb until we replaced them. Now, as far as the critical situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, the critical period, which was the autumn of 1992 and 1993 as well, so when they replaced me and brought in Miro Akmadzic as premier, who replaced Jure Pelivan and Mr. Lasic came into the Presidency at Izetbegovic's support unlawful, there in Zagreb "[Realtime transcript read 'in Greater Serbia'] there were two levers that they pulled so that the Presidency at one point in time was left without a single Croat in it. Of course, the Contact Group and the people who wanted to see an end to the conflict in Bosnia recommended first that the Presidency be rehabilitated as the foremost political body in the country. And Mr. Izetbegovic and the people that stayed on in the War Presidency, there was an empty Muslim seat, the seat of Fikret Abdic, and they brought in, by regular procedure, the third-placed person from the elections, Mr. Durakovic. I, as the first person, because I was the sole victor in the elections, I returned to the Presidency. And since Mr. Boras gave up on Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, the third man in the second place was Ivo Komsic, who, at the elections, gained that right. So, for the first time, the state was rehabilitated with its most important body, and it was to try and mitigate the effects of the previous policy that had been waged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, very quickly, back on line 7 of page 103, the transcript says "in Greater Serbia." I believe that your testimony was there was in Zagreb, two levers being pulled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you say just now, you mentioned Mr. Komsic, can you tell the Judges, please, was Mr. Komsic a Bosnian Croat?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Finally, sir --.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's indulgence, one more minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I appreciate your testimony. I don't mean to put you on the spot, but in light of the questions -- some of the questions that Mr. Praljak asked you, I must ask you about the fighting around Tomislavgrad, Livno, Bugojno, between Serb forces and the forces of the HVO. Do you have any recollection of the dates when that fighting occurred?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting occurred in several cycles. The first cycle was the autumn of 1992, and then when the HVO managed to defend most of the territory, in 1993 there were attempts to use the vacuum in the defence of Croatian territories, of course, with a tendency towards moving towards Split or to cut off the Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In light of this fighting, sir -- let me go specifically, excuse me. My last question to you will be: In reference to, for example, the fighting around Stolac, Capljina, Mostar in the period May to June, 1992, do you have any information as to how long the actual fighting occurred and how many casualties were suffered on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs did not supply any information even via the Red Cross. That could only be seen and established on the basis of images from Bijeljina, towns that were Serbian at the time, or Banja Luka. Suddenly you would see 30 obituaries and the citizens would say, "Where are these people? How come they died?" There wasn't a flu epidemic or something. So these were people coming in from -- to the Mostar battlefront from other areas and they died. There were a great many casualties, great many fatalities. But there was a lot of brutality later on, because General Perisic, who was the commander of those forces, was well known -- well, he was the equivalent of Ratko Mladic. There was no difference. This one was at liberty; the other one wasn't at liberty. That's the only difference. So it was a brutal time and this -- the survival of the HVO was important, because at Grahovo and Glamoc they had to break through a whole fortress set up by a professional Serb army. But they were great optimists and never believed that it would fall, so they did not set up a second and third defence line. And when the first line fell, they went as far as they could go on foot and in vehicles on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are other matters that I would like to be able to clarify and pursue, but in the interest of time, I will stop there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have just completed your testimony in The Hague. I'd like to thank you on behalf of the Bench for having come here today to testify on request of the Prosecution. As you know, we are going to be hearing another witness tomorrow. We'll see you at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
